articles.title: What is going on with gaming? [SyrupCast]
articles.text:
In this week’s episode of the SyrupCast, MobileSyrup’s EIC Jon Lamont is joined by gaming editor Brad Shankar and friend of the show and longtime MobileSyrup contributor Chris Brown to discuss the state of gaming.
Anyone who’s paid any attention to the gaming industry lately knows that things are crazy right now. From the end of physical media to shady acquisitions and, well, Xbox in general, things are a mess.
Brad and Chris walk us through everything going wrong in the industry right now, from its roots all the way back in the Xbox One era to the rampant layoffs and price hikes plaguing the industry now.
We discuss the impact of forever games, Game Pass, streaming, and more. Chris also discusses his experience with the new Gears of War: E-Day, the potential layoffs the team is staring down, and the value of institutional knowledge at game studios.
Finally, we wrap up by discussing bright spots in the industry and what Canadians can do to promote made-in-Canada games, and close by reminiscing about our favourite Xbox 360 titles.
Check out our previous SyrupCast episode here.

articles.title: OpenAI’s Jalapeño ASICs are deployed alongside AMD EPYC ‘Turin’ CPUs as hosts — Hardware VP says Nvidia’s Vera standalone is ‘a little bit behind… on that maturity level’
articles.text:
OpenAI’s Jalapeño ASICs are deployed alongside AMD EPYC ‘Turin’ CPUs as hosts — Hardware VP says Nvidia’s Vera standalone is ‘a little bit behind… on that maturity level’
Hardware VP Robert Ho says the choice to use Turin was “pragmatic.”
OpenAI’s new Jalapeño ASIC is being deployed internally alongside AMD EPYC Turin hosts, each with 1.5TB of memory. SemiAnalysis described the rack-scale deployment of Jalapeño following the reveal of the chip, which we asked Richard Ho, VP and Head of Hardware at OpenAI, about in an interview. Ho told us that the decision to use Turin was “pragmatic,” describing Nvidia’s new Vera CPU as “a little bit behind… on that maturity level.”
“The way we approached that design was really in terms of de-risking and being able to do that design fast. Vera, as a standalone, is a little bit behind on that maturity level. The Turing device is strong. It did what we needed to do, and partly our partners had some experience with it,” Ho told Tom’s Hardware Premium. “For the Jalapeño program, we were trying to make very pragmatic decisions. We wanted to be aggressive on the goals of the performance and the cost, but we didn’t want to take unnecessary risks. That felt like a good design decision that would fit within the parameters of how we make these design decisions."
There are many Arm-based CPUs on the market, many of which are deployed internally at different hyperscalers, such as Google Cloud’s Axiom and AWS’ Graviton, but Vera and Arm’s own AGI have been described as agentic CPUs, purportedly accelerating the complex reasoning involved in agentic loops compared to their x86 counterparts from AMD and Intel. We asked Ho about this dynamic, and why Turin was the right choice given the close working relationship between OpenAI and Nvidia, who responded with the quote above.
Arm has long touted the virtues of the AArch64 ISA compared to x86, going as far as to claim that its own AGI CPU provides more than twice the performance of modern x86 platforms. That claim is based on internal estimates, not real benchmarks, however. The company has been naturally bullish on AGI’s adoption in the market, though even with an impressive $2 billion in commitments, analysts say the market penetration will still be in the low single digits after two years.
With the explosion of server CPU demand this year and evolving agentic workloads, Nvidia has been at the forefront of messaging, comparing its Arm-based Vera to the x86 competition, boldly claiming a 1.8x improvement over a competing AMD Turin chip; a figure that’s extracted from an overall benchmark suite showing Vera just 3% ahead of AMD’s EPYC 9755.
Many semi-custom Arm designs, from Graviton to Azure’s Cobalt, have focused on core density and efficiency for cloud workloads. Vera and AGI are a shift toward messaging against peak performance. In early Vera benchmarks, Nvidia’s CPU looks impressive, though we’ve yet to see the chip in action in a wide variety of workloads, much less benchmarked against AMD’s upcoming Venice CPUs or Intel’s Diamond Rapids.
What’s interesting about OpenAI’s decision to use Turin is that it’s one of Arm’s deployment partners for AGI, as well as among the list of customers “exploring the Vera CPU,” according to Nvidia. OpenAI, other frontier labs, and hyperscalers keep a wide variety of hardware in their fleet. Pairing Jalapeño specifically with Turin came down to reducing risk, with Ho pointing to the maturity of the platform.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Broadly, x86_64 is more mature than AArch64; ARM has been around since the mid-1980’s, though a proper 64-bit extension didn’t arrive until 12 years after it was introduced on x86. And although Arm has worked its way into data centers over the past two decades, there’s still a much deeper x86 foundation reaching back several decades.
It doesn’t seem Ho’s comments were specifically on the delineation between AArch64 and x86, however. Rather, the comments are focused on the dynamic between Turin and Vera, with the latter being Nvidia’s first foray into a custom CPU core for the data center. Although the early benchmarks of Vera are impressive, it nonetheless represented an unnecessary risk for OpenAI’s rack-scale Jalapeño deployment.
Ho’s comments about OpenAI’s partners having experience with Turin expose where the thinking for the hardware team was at, as well. There are some differences in the practicality of servicing the host system between Turin and Vera, most notably the fact that Vera is board-mounted while Turin chips are socketed; swapping chips isn’t common in a server regardless, but it’s easier with Turin.
Given that OpenAI has a fleet of hardware available, it’s possible Jalapeño will be deployed with a different host system in the future, potentially paired with Arm’s AGI or Nvidia’s Vera. For now, however, Turin was the right choice.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Googles Rechenzentren im All: Warum dafür 1.800 Starship-Starts nötig sind
articles.text:
Googles Rechenzentren im All: Warum 1.800 Starship-Starts nötig sind
Google hat im Rahmen seines „Project Suncatcher“ erstmals einen eigenen KI-Chip ins All geschickt. Wie Techcrunch berichtet, umkreist die Hardware an Bord eines Satelliten die Erde, um den Aufbau von Rechenzentren im Weltraum vorzubereiten.
Den Trägersatelliten baute das Unternehmen Planet Labs aus San Francisco im US-Bundesstaat Kalifornien. Er soll testen, ob Googles Tensor Processing Units (TPU) im Orbit arbeiten, da Labortests am Boden den Einsatz im All laut Projektleiter Travis Beals nicht vollständig simulieren können.
Aktuell rechnet der Chip nur in kurzen Intervallen von 15 Minuten. Ein Dauerbetrieb würde die Stromversorgung und die Kühlung des kleinen Satelliten überlasten. Da es im All keine Luft gibt, kann die Hitze der Chips nicht über herkömmliche Lüfter abgeleitet werden, sondern muss abstrahlen. Spätere Systeme werden im Produktivbetrieb daher den Einsatz großflächiger Radiatoren erfordern, um nicht zu überhitzen.
Das Projekt Suncatcher soll langfristig zu orbitalen Netzwerken aus Dutzenden Satelliten führen. Ob diese Vision jemals den Testbetrieb verlässt, entscheidet sich letztlich in der kaufmännischen Betrachtung.
Die wirtschaftliche Hürde für orbitale Datenzentren
Damit der Betrieb von Hardware im Weltraum finanziell mit irdischen Anlagen konkurrieren kann, müssen die Startkosten in den niedrigen Erdorbit auf unter 200 US-Dollar pro Kilogramm fallen. Die Forscher:innen leiten diese harte Preisgrenze in einer vorab auf dem Preprint-Server Arxiv (PDF) veröffentlichten Studie, die demnächst auch im Fachmagazin Joule erscheinen soll, direkt aus den aktuellen Energiekosten terrestrischer Rechenzentren ab.
Weitere Details zu dem Konzept erläutert das Unternehmen in einem begleitenden Beitrag auf dem hauseigenen Forschungsblog. Um diesen Zielwert zu erreichen, benötigt Google massive Unterstützung durch seinen Launch-Partner SpaceX. Das Raumfahrtunternehmen konnte seine Preise immerhin seit dem ersten Start der Falcon-1-Rakete kontinuierlich reduzieren. Laut der Analyse sinken die Kosten um etwa 20 Prozent mit jeder Verdopplung der insgesamt ins All beförderten Frachtmenge.
Setzt sich dieser Skaleneffekt fort, müssen weitere 370.000 Tonnen Material in den Orbit transportiert werden, um den anvisierten Preis von 200 Dollar pro Kilogramm zu realisieren. Legt man die geplante Kapazität der neuen Schwerlastrakete zugrunde, entspricht das etwa 1.800 Flügen des Starships.
Bei einer Auslastung von 200 Tonnen pro Flug und einer Verteilung auf zehn Jahre wären das 180 Starts pro Jahr. Diese Frequenz läge deutlich über den derzeitigen Startraten der gesamten Raumfahrtindustrie.
Sonnensynchrone Orbits als Energiequelle für Satelliten
Neben den Transportkosten behandelt die Studie die Energieversorgung der Satelliten. Um das Potenzial der Sonne zu nutzen, die weit mehr Energie liefert, als die Menschheit auf der Erde verbraucht, sieht das Konzept den Betrieb der Satelliten in einem sonnensynchronen Dämmerungsorbit (Dawn-Dusk-Orbit) vor.
Auf dieser Flugbahn bewegt sich ein Satellit exakt entlang der irdischen Tag-Nacht-Grenze und bleibt dadurch fast ununterbrochen im direkten Sonnenlicht. Das erhöht die Produktivität der Paneele im Vergleich zu irdischen Installationen in mittleren Breiten um den Faktor acht. Gleichzeitig reduziert der konstante Lichteinfall den Bedarf an schweren Batteriespeichern an Bord der Satelliten.
Die technische Architektur der Satelliten-Cluster
Moderne KI-Systeme tauschen beachtliche Datenmengen aus, wofür kommerzielle Satellitennetzwerke aktuell nicht die nötigen Bandbreiten bieten. Als Lösung sollen Gruppen von jeweils 81 Satelliten sehr nah beieinander fliegen, gebündelt in einer Formation mit nur einem Kilometer Radius.
Durch diese geringe Distanz lassen sich handelsübliche Laser-Bauteile für den Datenaustausch nutzen, um Übertragungsraten im Terabit-Bereich zu erreichen. Der sonst sehr hohe Energiebedarf für Laser-Verbindungen über große Entfernungen im All entfällt auf diese Weise.
Strahlenbelastung und Silent Data Corruption bei TPUs
Eine Hürde ist die kosmische Strahlung. Um die Bedingungen im All zu simulieren, hat Google seine Chips in einem Teilchenbeschleuniger der US-amerikanischen Universität von Kalifornien getestet. Die Versuche zeigten, dass die Hardware die dauerhafte Strahlenbelastung besser verträgt als zunächst angenommen.
Problematisch können jedoch einzelne energiereiche Teilchen aus dem dauerhaften Strahlenbeschuss im Orbit sein, wenn sie bei einem Treffer auf dem Chip unbemerkt Daten verändern. Wenden die Prozessoren lediglich fertige KI-Modelle an, passiert das nur bei etwa einer von einer Million Rechenoperationen, was in der Forschung als vertretbar gilt.
Beim Training neuer KI-Modelle ist diese schleichende Datenverfälschung jedoch ein ungelöstes Problem. Für diesen Fall müssen Tausende Prozessoren über Monate hinweg fehlerfrei zusammenarbeiten, um brauchbare Ergebnisse zu liefern.
Google arbeitet bereits an weiteren Prototypen, die den Datenaustausch per Laser im Verbund testen sollen. Der Start dieser vernetzten Satelliten ist ab Anfang 2027 geplant.

articles.title: Research roundup: 6 cool science stories we almost missed
articles.text:
It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. September’s list includes a tantalizing hint of the elusive dark matter at the LUX-ZEPLIN detector; entangled Z bosons at the Large Hadron Collider; possible use of psychoactive substances in the Late Pleistocene; and an intriguing technical description of a telescope attributed to Galileo.
A hint of dark matter?
Physicists believe dark matter makes up roughly 85 percent of matter in our universe, with the strongest (but not only) candidate being so-called weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs). But directly detecting WIMPs, or other alternative hypothetical dark matter particles, has eluded physicists for decades. We might have our first glimpse, however, courtesy of the LUX-ZEPLIN detector buried deep in a gold mine in South Dakota. Those potentially exciting results were presented in a scientific talk at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics conference in Japan, with a preprint available on the arXiv. (It has been submitted to Physical Review Letters for peer review.)
The announcement came with strong caveats: the signal is just a hint, well below the threshold needed to confirm discovery, and might just be a statistical fluke. Anyone who regularly follows dark matter news knows that past tantalizing anomalies evaporated as more data came in. But the LUX-ZEPLIN team was unable to account for this event and decided to report their result to the broader physics community. They are still collecting data, as is the XENONnT at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy. And China’s PandaX detector is currently being built.
If it turns out to be a WIMP that struck a xenon nucleus, it’s not what physicists would predict. The event had a higher nuclear recoil energy than expected, which means the detector should have also picked up several lower-energy WIMPs; it did not. That has theoreticians scrambling to come up with alternative models. Perhaps the interaction rate increases with collision energy. Or perhaps WIMPs have an internal structure, like an atom, and only interact if hit hard enough. Or its coupling to ordinary matter could depend on its momentum.
Cornell University physicist N. David Mermin once described quantum entanglement as “the closest thing we have to magic,” since it means that disturbances in one part of the universe can instantly affect distant other parts of the universe, somehow bypassing the cosmic speed-of-light limit. Albert Einstein memorably dubbed it “spooky action at a distance.” Today, entanglement is the foundation for quantum computing and next-generation sensors, among other applications.
Maintaining quantum entanglement is usually a delicate process; any interference can cause entangled particles to decohere quickly. Despite this, in 2023, physicists found evidence of entanglement between pairs of top quarks produced at the Large Hadron Collider’s ATLAS experiment, raising the possibility that large colliders could be used as an investigative tool to study spooky action at a distance. Now ATLAS physicists have observed entanglement in pairs of Z bosons, according to a paper published in the journal Physical Review Letters.
Z bosons are produced when a Higgs boson decays and are themselves extremely short-lived particles, decaying into pairs of electrons and muons. The ATLAS detector precisely tracks those decay patterns. The physicists used that data to reconstruct the angles at which electrons and muons were emitted to infer the spins of the original Z bosons that preceded them. The authors claim that this is the highest-energy example of entanglement observed to date
Dreams of colonizing Mars face many significant obstacles given the harsh conditions (for humans) on the red planet—including housing. Transporting anything from Earth to Mars is costly, and building materials are especially so. That’s why Hong Kong engineers devised a recipe to combine Martian rocks with terrestrial gelatin and yeast, which then hardens into a durable “living” building material on par with cheap concrete, according to a paper published in the journal Chem Circularity.
Co-author Jishen Qiu of The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology drew inspiration from the hardening of freeze-dried fruits, noting that the Martian environment has extremely low temperatures and pressures akin to freeze-drying. The team experimented with various mixtures of sand and glue, the latter made from gelatin and yeast. But it’s a special yeast coated with sticky proteins similar to those mussels use to adhere to rocky surfaces. The gelatin provides scaffolding for the cells to grow, and the sand provides the structure and mass. Qiu et al. tested their concoction in simulated Martian conditions, 3D-printing small domes the size of wine corks.
They found that the mixture freeze-dries after exiting the nozzle, leaving a light, porous foam with a compressive strength of 10 to 12 megapascals. Per the authors, that is strong enough to build a one- or two-story structure on Earth, where gravity is three times stronger than on Mars, so it should be possible to use their material to make much higher structures on the red planet. It’s less energy-intensive than heating and melting Martian rocks or moon dust into bricks, another approach that’s been proposed. And yeast recovered from dismantled structures could be easily recycled to build new ones.
There is ample evidence that humans in many cultures throughout history used various hallucinogenic substances in religious ceremonies or shamanic rituals, at least since the Neolithic period and the advent of farming and fermented alcoholic drinks (like barley beer). That includes not just ancient Egypt but also ancient Greek, Vedic, Maya, Inca, and Aztec cultures. For instance, in 2024, archaeologists found that an ancient Egyptian vase in the shape of the deity Bes showed traces of chemical plant compounds known to produce hallucinations. And in 2022, archaeologists uncovered evidence that an ancient Peruvian people laced the beer served at their feasts with hallucinogens.
Now Griffith University archaeologists have discovered that humans might have been using mind-altering subsances—by sucking and chewing on betel nuts—as early as the Late Pleistocene period some 25,000 years ago, according to a paper published in Science Advances. Betel nut consumption is common in India and the South Pacific, usually by mixing the seed with slaked lime (which releases the psychoactive compounds) and a few other ingredients to make a “quid,” then chewing it. The effects include mild euphoria and high alertness.
The Griffith team discovered two rare early human forager skeletons from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, concluding that one dated to 25,000 to 16,000 years ago and the other to 7,600–6,300 years ago. Both skeletons had deep rounded grooves in their teeth, apparently caused by constantly sucking on whole betel nuts. By soaking betel nuts in artificial saliva, the authors concluded that this would release enough arecoline to alter brain function, although the psychoactive effects would be milder.
The authors posit that people from that period sucked on betel nuts to relieve tooth pain, given that these populations are known to have had bad teeth and arecoline is a natural analgesic. But the seeds are abrasive and, over time, wore down the foragers’ teeth so much that inner pulp chambers were exposed. “So while this habit may have been a remedy for toothache, years of prolonged nut-sucking eventually caused much worse dental health problems, creating a cycle of continued habitual use,” said co-author Adam Brumm.
Historians generally agree that a German-born eyeglass manufacturer in the Netherlands, Hans Lippershey, invented the first bona fide telescope in the 1590s. Similar instruments made by other inventors soon popped up, and by 1609, people could buy “spyglasses” in local shops in Paris. Within a few months, the phenomenon had spread to Italy and caught the attention of Galileo Galilei, who fashioned his own telescopes to make ground-breaking astronomical observations that helped the Copernican model of the solar system supplant the Ptolemaic worldview that had dominated for centuries.
Galileo swore never to sell any of his telescopes, and he didn’t document any technical analyses of his instruments either; only eight such telescopes survive; none can unequivocally be attributed to the astronomer. But a historian at the University of Limerick in Ireland has uncovered a previously unknown 17th century description of a four-lens telescope attributed to Galileo in a 1666 manuscript written by a Spanish Dominican friar, detailing his findings in a paper published in the journal Annals of Science.
The text in question is De Tellescopiis Stellarum, by Friar Ignacio Muñoz. Author Jose Maria Moreno Madrid was perusing the treatise when he came across the friar’s analysis of the telescope, complete with diagrams and drawings of the instrument. The analysis was specifically requested by the viceroy of New Spain as a test of the friar’s scientific expertise. Muñoz proposed improvements to the Spanish fleet to King Philip IV in hopes of ending his exile to Portuguese India. Muñoz noted in his manuscript that the telescope belonged to the king and was made by Galileo.
According to Madrid, Galileo had presented Philip IV and his wife with one large and two smaller telescopes to curry favor while working on the problem of longitude. So Muñoz’s description could be referring to one of those three telescopes. The first four-lens telescopes appeared around 1643, but if Madrid’s analysis is correct, this would mean the innovation occurred much earlier, in 1630 at the latest, and could be attributed to Galileo. And Muñoz’s 1666 description would be “the most detailed technical analysis of a telescope provenly made” by the Renaissance astronomer.
Peep shows, aka raree shows, were wildly popular in 17th and 18th century Europe as a form of immersive entertainment by traveling showmen. Pictures or objects were mounted inside a box or wooden cabinet and viewed through a small hole or magnifying glass, creating the illusion of depth perception, sometimes illuminated with candles to create special lighting effects. By the 19th century, peep shows had evolved into cosmoramas, collected in galleries housed in urban bazaars across Britain and Ireland. The cosmoramas weren’t just used for entertainment, but also as a real estate marketing tool, according to a paper published in the journal Early Popular Visual Culture.
John Plunkett, a historian at the University of Exeter, was researching the history of cosmoramas and similar visual technology in the UK and Ireland as part of a broader European project. While poring over advertisements and articles in newspaper archives from the 1820s onward, in order to map the emerging use of cosmoramas around the world, he stumbled on a London auctioneer and surveyor, Brooks and Hedger, who were using cosmoramas in the 1830s to market various estate properties for sale, offering views of homes and grounds including “aerial perspectives.”
Their offices were on Old Bond Street, close to the Cosmorama Rooms of Regent Street, so clearly the firm was capitalizing on the current fad. Per Plunkett, producing cosmoramas would have been a costly investment for the firm, requiring an artist to visit each property and create paintings or drawings from different angles, so this strategy was likely reserved for estates and luxury properties. The practice seems to have been abandoned by 1860, but Plunkett likened it to the virtual tours or walkthroughs employed by online real estate listing services like Redfin, Zillow, or Rightmove in the UK.
Jennifer is a senior writer at Ars Technica with a particular focus on where science meets culture, covering everything from physics and related interdisciplinary topics to her favorite films and TV series. Jennifer lives in Baltimore with her spouse, physicist Sean M. Carroll, and their two cats, Ariel and Caliban.

articles.title: Sean Parker is rebuilding Stability AI around music | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Sean Parker, the Napster co-founder, has jumped back into the music industry, and he tells The Information that he’s playing by the rules this time. (Asking for forgiveness rather than permission didn’t work out so well last time around, he readily concedes.)
Two years ago, he joined an $80 million rescue of Stability AI, the image-generator startup that nearly collapsed after overspending and internal turmoil led to founder Emad Mostaque’s ouster. Now Parker and his longtime friend Prem Akkaraju, who became CEO, are taking the wraps off what they’ve been building.
The big idea, Parker says, is to turn Stability into the go-to AI toolmaker for music professionals. Toward that end, in late August, the company announced $76 million in funding from, among others, Sony, Warner, and Universal, which also licensed their catalogs for training as part of the deal. Stability has since released three new audio models and AI music-editing software. The AI can generate whole instrumental tracks or short snippets from text prompts. Parker says an upcoming update will let users hum a melody or beatbox a drum pattern to steer it.

articles.title: Donald Trump a interrogé Grok sur les effets d'une capture de Maduro au Venezuela, un mois avant de l'ordonner
articles.text:
Le 3 janvier 2026, les États-Unis lançaient une opération éclair au Venezuela, au cours de laquelle l’armée américaine capturait Nicolás Maduro. Pendant un temps, la question s’est posée de savoir si un mème avait poussé Donald Trump à autoriser une telle expédition. On sait désormais que Donald Trump avait aussi interrogé Grok, le chatbot d’Elon Musk, un mois avant l’opération.
C’est en tout cas ce qui ressort d’un long papier consacré à Donald Trump paru dans les colonnes du Time ce jeudi 1er octobre. Le portrait publié par le magazine américain s’appuie notamment sur un entretien de 75 minutes dans le Bureau ovale. Dans un passage sur l’intelligence artificielle, le journaliste Eric Cortellessa raconte une rencontre discrète entre le président et Elon Musk à la Maison-Blanche, en décembre 2025.
Une discussion avec Grok un mois avant
Lors de cette rencontre, raconte le Time, le président américain a passé des heures à interroger Grok, le chatbot de xAI, l’entreprise d’IA de Musk. Il lui aurait notamment demandé comment les Vénézuéliens réagiraient si les États-Unis capturaient Nicolás Maduro. Trump a donc interrogé un assistant grand public, intégré au réseau social X, sur les effets d’une opération militaire, un mois avant de la lancer.
Ce passage repose sur un seul témoin, un responsable présent ce jour-là, que le Time ne nomme pas. D’après ce qu’il a rapporté, Grok a répondu que Maduro était un dictateur répressif et profondément impopulaire dans son pays. Le chatbot a ajouté que beaucoup de Vénézuéliens fêteraient sans doute sa chute, toujours selon ce responsable. Après la capture, des Vénézuéliens ont bien fêté la chute de Maduro, notamment dans la diaspora, même si de fausses images et vidéos ont aussi circulé sur les réseaux sociaux.
Au moment de cet échange, Donald Trump faisait déjà frapper, depuis septembre 2025, des bateaux vénézuéliens qu’il accusait de transporter de la drogue. Un mois plus tard, l’armée américaine frappait Caracas et capturait Maduro. Celui-ci a été emmené manu militari à New York pour y être jugé pour narcoterrorisme.
Il n’est pas dit, dans l’article du Time, à quel point l’analyse de Grok a pesé sur la décision d’attaque, à supposer que le chatbot ait eu une influence. D’après des responsables cités par le Time, le président américain en a tout de même conclu, après les scènes de joie dans les rues, que Grok était « ingénieux ». Il n’est pas précisé si Trump utilisait Grok avant cette affaire ou s’il s’en sert depuis pour accompagner ou valider des décisions.
Le Time décrit un président de plus en plus séduit par l’IA et par les patrons qui la développent. En septembre, Trump a présenté une tenue de la Space Force générée par IA. Il veut aussi rebaptiser l’intelligence artificielle « Super Intelligence ». Ce mardi 29 septembre, il a reçu à la Maison-Blanche les dirigeants de six grandes entreprises du secteur. Ils y ont signé une « constitution » par laquelle ils s’engagent à s’autoréguler, sans contrôle de l’État.
Les Américains sont beaucoup moins enthousiastes que leur président. D’après un sondage CNN réalisé par l’institut SSRS et cité par le Time, 75 % d’entre eux voient l’IA avec plus de crainte que d’enthousiasme. Les électeurs des deux camps réclament aussi davantage de contrôle fédéral.

articles.title: De la Kindle de base à la Colorsoft, Amazon renouvelle (presque) toutes ses liseuses
articles.text:
De la Kindle de base à la Colorsoft, Amazon renouvelle (presque) toutes ses liseuses
La Kindle soufflera ses 20 bougies en 2027, et Amazon prépare le terrain. La firme renouvelle d'un coup ses trois liseuses phares, avec châssis unibody, écrans affleurants et nouvelles teintes. Seule la Scribe ne profite pas du vent de renouveau.
Amazon ne fait pas les choses à moitié cette fois. Plutôt que de rafraîchir un modèle isolé comme il en a parfois l'habitude, le géant du e-commerce rénove simultanément la Kindle de base, la Kindle Paperwhite et la Kindle Colorsoft, cette dernière étant pour mémoire la première liseuse couleur de la marque, lancée en 2024. Les points communs de cette cuvée sont la finesse et l'homogénéité. Toutes adoptent un design unibody, décliné en plastique ou en aluminium selon les versions, ainsi qu'un écran désormais affleurant, sans le rebord caractéristique des générations précédentes. La Scribe n'est pas concernée par les annonces du jour. Mais Amazon avait annoncée une Scribe Colosoft pour le marché françaisen mai dernier.
Plus fins, plus légers, et un bouton qui change de place
Les chiffres parlent d'eux-mêmes. La Kindle de base descend à 140 g, contre 158 g pour sa prédécesseuse, tandis que la Paperwhite passe de 211 g à 204 g. Les deux affichent 6,8 mm d'épaisseur, soit 1 mm de moins qu'auparavant. La Colorsoft suit la même cure d'amincissement, avec elle aussi une façade affleurante. Notez par ailleurs que le bouton d'alimentation migre du bas de l'appareil vers le côté supérieur droit sur l'ensemble de la gamme.
Un écran affleurant sur une liseuse pose toutefois un problème évident, celui des touches accidentelles quand on tient l'appareil à pleine main. Amazon y répond par une zone morte capacitive dynamique. « Quand vous tenez le Kindle, où que vous posiez le pouce, il détecte de lui-même une zone morte dans la couche tactile capacitive. Il se réajuste, tout simplement, et il sait que le doigt est là », explique Kevin Keith, vice-président des appareils chez Amazon. Il faudra voir ce que ça donne à l'usage. La marque applique également une couche noire entre les bords des dalles, une technique inédite chez elle qui évite que la couleur de la coque ne déborde visuellement sur l'écran.
Côté coloris, la Kindle de base en plastique se décline en Graphite et en Ube, un violet inédit, tandis que sa version aluminium arrive en Alpine Sky et Seaglass Green. La Paperwhite Signature Edition reprend Graphite et Seaglass Green, et la Colorsoft Signature Edition propose Graphite et Fig, une teinte bordeaux.
Des pages qui tournent "30 % plus vite"
On nous promet également qu'il sera possible de tourner les pages 30 % plus rapidement qu'avec la génération précédente. La Kindle de base conserve un écran e-paper de 15,2 cm (6 pouces) et une autonomie de six semaines. La Paperwhite et la Colorsoft montent à 17,8 cm (7 pouces), et la première double la mise avec douze semaines d'autonomie, un éclairage chaud réglable, un contraste supérieur et une conception étanche.
Les versions Signature Edition, en aluminium avec 32 Go de stockage, ajoutent un éclairage frontal à ajustement automatique, une fonction de double tapotement pour tourner les pages et des connecteurs pogo. Attention toutefois, ces connecteurs ne servent qu'à relier un socle de charge vendu séparément. Pas de recharge sans fil au programme donc.
L'aluminium des châssis est recyclé à 80 % nous apprend le communiqué de presse, et les nouvelles Kindle se conforment à la réglementation européenne sur les batteries, ce qui signifie que celles-ci sont remplaçables par l'utilisateur. Un vrai progrès pour la durée de vie de ces appareils.
Prix, disponibilité et accessoires
Enfin, côté tarifs, ils sont logiquement nombreux, au regard de la quantité de références :
• à partir de 154,99 euros pour la Kindle 2026
• à partir de 194,99 euros pour la Kindle Aluminium 2026
• à partir de 209,99 euros pour la Kindle Paperwhite 2026
• à partir de 259,99 euros pour la Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition 2026
• à partir de 299,99 euros pour la Kindle Colorsoft 2026
• à partir de 329,99 euros pour la Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition 2026
Tous ces nouveaux modèles sont d'ores et déjà disponbiles. Amazon accompagne en outre cette fournée d'accessoires maison. Le Kindle Click, une télécommande Bluetooth de tourne-page rechargeable en USB-C, fonctionne avec les Kindle de 2024 et ultérieurs et coûte 34,99 euros. L'Étui avec boutons de changement de page intégrés, une coque à boutons réservée aux Signature Edition via leurs connecteurs pogo, est affichée à 79,99 euros, le socle de charge à 54,99 euros et l'étui folio du Kindle aluminium à 44,99 euros.

articles.title: OpenAI DevDay 2026 Recap for Developers
articles.text:
OpenAI announced a series of product and developer updates at DevDay 2026, including GPT-6.1 Sol, computer use for the Agents API, cloud-based Codex environments, a Decisions API, and new plugin capabilities for ChatGPT.
For developers building agents, the Agents API now supports computer use, allowing applications to operate software through graphical interfaces. The API also incorporates multi-agent capabilities from Codex, tool search, tool calling, and context compaction, with OpenAI managing the underlying execution infrastructure. The functionality is available through the API and in Codex and ChatGPT Work for selected plans.
OpenAI also released GPT-6.1 Sol, an update to GPT-6 Sol aimed at coding, computer use, and professional tasks. OpenAI says the model approaches GPT-6 Astra on several evaluations while charging one-fifth of Astra's standard input and output token prices. Cached input costs $0.10 per million tokens. GPT-6.1 Sol is available through the API, ChatGPT Work, and Codex.
Codex can now run in cloud environments in addition to local computers, allowing developers to start remote tasks from other devices. OpenAI also updated the Codex CLI with voice input and an /agents interface for delegating and monitoring multiple tasks. A new code-review workflow can analyze diffs and potential issues in GitHub pull requests and GitLab merge requests, while Codex Security Cloud can scan repositories and new commits, investigate findings, remove duplicates, and prepare fixes.
Another developer release is the Decisions API, currently in limited preview. It uses the smaller Luna model to select from a predefined set of answers based on text or image context. OpenAI positions the API for tasks such as classification, request routing, and choosing an agent's next action.
OpenAI also expanded ChatGPT's plugin system. Developers can now build sidebar experiences, interactive conversation panels, and custom file viewers. Plugins can also respond to events through the proposed MCP Events specification, allowing automations to start when an event occurs in a connected application.
DevDay also introduced Dots, persistent agents that can work on ongoing tasks, and ChatGPT Space, a shared workspace where teams and agents can work with common context. Together with the developer releases, these changes extend OpenAI's platform from individual model calls toward persistent agents that can use tools, operate software, collaborate, and execute tasks remotely.
Community discussion focused on the growing emphasis on agents and developer infrastructure. Developers highlighted computer use, cloud-based Codex, and lower-cost models as practical additions, while others questioned whether the releases represented significant advances over capabilities already available across existing agent platforms.
OpenAI Developer Victor Nunez shared:
You would not believe just how much better dots got in a single week pre DevDay. I expect this to become the favorite way of interacting with AI for most people.
Meanwhile developer @TokenGremlin posted:
Thinking about it more, I actually think GPT-6.1 Sol might be THE BEST release in OpenAI’s history. It gave me a really unusual feeling that I almost never get from a model: Luna pricing, Astra-level quality.
DevDay 2026 showed OpenAI moving beyond individual model interactions toward persistent agent workflows. With autonomous agents, lower-cost models, cloud-based coding, and expanded ChatGPT integrations, the company is building infrastructure for agents that can work continuously across applications and tasks.

articles.title: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot : ce que les IA gratuites vous prennent en échange — Frandroid
articles.text:
ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude et Copilot s’utilisent tous sans sortir la carte bancaire. Aucun n’est gratuit pour autant. Chacun se rembourse à sa manière : avec de la publicité, avec vos conversations réinjectées dans l’entraînement de ses modèles, ou avec un modèle moins puissant que celui réservé aux abonnés.
Le site allemand Notebookcheck, connu pour ses tests de PC portables et de smartphones, a vérifié tout ça service par service dans un comparatif publié ce mercredi 30 septembre, puis traduit en français. Chez ChatGPT et Gemini, la collecte des conversations est activée par défaut.
Si vous n’avez jamais ouvert les réglages, vous avez déjà dit oui sans le savoir.
ChatGPT et Gemini se servent par défaut
Commençons par ChatGPT. La version gratuite donne accès à des conversations textuelles illimitées avec GPT-5.6 Luna. Le plus récent GPT-6 Luna n’est proposé aux comptes gratuits que dans l’application de bureau. La vraie limite se situe dans la fenêtre de contexte, c’est-à-dire la quantité de texte que le modèle peut lire d’un coup : 27 000 tokens, soit environ 12 pages selon OpenAI. C’est deux fois moins que les formules Go (8 euros par mois) et Plus (23 euros). Un long contrat ou un mémoire ne tient donc pas en une seule fois.
Depuis fin août, la version gratuite affiche aussi des publicités en Europe, et la formule Go à 8 euros n’y échappe pas. Pour l’instant, ces annonces ne sont pas personnalisées dans l’Espace économique européen ni en Suisse. On peut les couper sans payer, via l’option « Réduire les limites de messages » dans Paramètres puis Contrôle des publicités. En échange, on a moins de messages et on perd la génération d’images et la recherche approfondie.
Par défaut, vos conversations servent aussi à entraîner les modèles d’OpenAI. Le bouton « Améliorer le modèle pour tout le monde », dans Paramètres puis Contrôle des données, est activé par défaut sur les comptes gratuits. Pour une question ponctuelle, la conversation temporaire échappe à l’entraînement. OpenAI en garde quand même une copie jusqu’à 30 jours pour des raisons de sécurité.
Même avec l’option coupée, noter une réponse d’un pouce levé ou baissé autorise OpenAI à utiliser toute la conversation concernée pour entraîner ses modèles.
Google propose l’offre gratuite la plus fournie des quatre : Gemini 3.6 Flash, un accès limité à Gemini 3.1 Pro, Deep Research, la génération d’images et Gemini Live. La formule Google AI Plus, à 4,99 euros par mois, sert surtout à doubler les limites. Malgré le poids de la publicité dans ses revenus, Google affirme dans son centre de confidentialité que les conversations avec Gemini ne servent pas à afficher des annonces.
Côté données, l’option « Keep Activity » est activée par défaut pour les plus de 18 ans, et des évaluateurs humains, y compris chez des prestataires externes, lisent une partie des conversations. Ces conversations relues sont conservées jusqu’à trois ans, même si vous supprimez votre activité. Google conseille lui-même de ne rien y écrire de confidentiel.
Couper « Keep Activity » ne règle pas tout pour autant : Google garde quand même les nouvelles conversations 72 heures. Attention aussi aux Gems, ces versions personnalisées de Gemini. Ils deviennent des « skills » en novembre, et les skills ne fonctionnent qu’avec cette option activée. Personnaliser son assistant revient donc à accepter la collecte.
Pour une question sensible ponctuelle, Gemini propose aussi une conversation temporaire, sans avoir à couper « Keep Activity » ni à renoncer aux skills. Google la conserve 72 heures, comme les conversations passées avec l’option désactivée.
Claude et Copilot, des réglages à aller chercher
Chez Anthropic, l’offre gratuite vient de s’étoffer. Depuis ce lundi 28 septembre, elle donne accès à Claude Sonnet 5.5 et Haiku 4.5, avec la mémoire entre les conversations et les applications connectées. Le haut de gamme Opus 5.5 reste en revanche réservé aux abonnés, avec une formule Pro à 18 euros par mois, ou 15 euros en paiement annuel.
Sur les données, Anthropic est moins transparent qu’on pourrait l’attendre d’une entreprise qui a construit son image sur la sécurité de l’IA. Ses pages d’aide ne disent pas si l’option « Help improve our AI models » est activée par défaut. Mieux vaut donc vérifier soi-même, dans Paramètres puis Confidentialité. Une fois l’option coupée, Anthropic promet de ne plus utiliser les nouvelles conversations. Les données déjà intégrées à un entraînement terminé ou en cours y restent, et les échanges repérés par ses filtres de sécurité peuvent encore servir à détecter les abus.
Microsoft prend la direction opposée et rogne sa version gratuite. Deep Research a quitté l’application grand public de Copilot le 18 août, et la fonction qui le remplace est payante. Côté données, l’entraînement se coupe à tout moment, mais Copilot conserve les conversations 18 mois par défaut.
Le plus gênant concerne la publicité. D’après Microsoft, les annonces personnalisées de Copilot peuvent s’appuyer sur l’historique de vos conversations et sur les souvenirs enregistrés. Pour les couper, direction Paramètres, puis Personnalisation, où il faut désactiver « Autoriser la personnalisation des publicités ».
Microsoft propose aussi, dans son tableau de bord de confidentialité, un bouton distinct qui coupe la personnalisation des publicités sur tous ses services d’un coup. Les comptes de moins de 18 ans ne voient jamais d’annonces personnalisées dans Copilot.
Microsoft recentre Copilot sur le travail. Bloomberg parlait dès mars de la « crise d’identité » de l’assistant, au moment où Microsoft réorganisait ses équipes Copilot. Fin septembre, Microsoft a présenté une nouvelle version de Copilot dans laquelle Word, Excel et PowerPoint s’ouvrent directement. Elle arrive d’abord chez les abonnés Microsoft 365 et dans les entreprises inscrites au programme de test. Satya Nadella, le patron de Microsoft, la décrit comme « un nouveau système d’exploitation pour le travail ».
    Pour aller plus loin
Copilot devient un « OS » selon Microsoft : chat, code et agents réunis
            
Payer un abonnement ne protège pas non plus vos conversations. Pour OpenAI, ChatGPT fait partie des services pour particuliers dont les contenus peuvent servir à l’entraînement, abonnés compris. Seules les offres Business, Enterprise, Edu et l’API, l’accès réservé aux développeurs, sont exclues par défaut. Anthropic applique la même logique, avec un bouton unique pour Claude Free, Pro et Max.
| Assistant | Publicité | Entraînement sur les conversations | Limites de la version gratuite | 
|---|---|---|---|
| ChatGPT | Oui (Free et Go), non personnalisée en Europe pour l’instant | Activé par défaut (Paramètres, Contrôle des données) | 27 000 tokens de contexte, GPT-6 Luna seulement dans l’application de bureau | 
| Gemini | Conversations non utilisées pour la publicité, selon Google | « Keep Activity » activé par défaut, conservation jusqu’à trois ans des conversations relues | Accès limité à Gemini 3.1 Pro | 
| Claude | Aucune signalée | Réglage par défaut non précisé (Paramètres, Confidentialité) | Opus 5.5 réservé aux abonnés | 
| Copilot | Oui, personnalisable à partir de vos conversations | Désactivable à tout moment, conservation de 18 mois par défaut | Deep Research retiré le 18 août | 
Avant de confier à un assistant une question de santé, un contrat ou des informations sur votre entreprise, passez cinq minutes dans les réglages. Les quatre services permettent de couper l’entraînement sur vos conversations sans payer.
Si vous jonglez entre plusieurs assistants, réservez les sujets sensibles à celui où l’entraînement est coupé. Le même réflexe vaut chez Meta, qui permet aussi de refuser que son IA exploite vos données Facebook et Instagram.
Enfin, la solution la plus extrême est de passer à l’IA locale. C’est possible, à condition d’avoir un ordinateur assez puissant et d’accepter des modèles moins performants que ceux de ChatGPT, Gemini ou Claude.
    Pour aller plus loin
Comment installer un modèle LLM type ChatGPT sur PC ou Mac en local ? Voici le guide ultime pour tous

articles.title: Micro Center Reportedly Requires ID and a Signed No-Export Declaration for RTX 5090 Sales
articles.text:
Friday, October 2nd 2026
Micro Center Reportedly Requires ID and a Signed No-Export Declaration for RTX 5090 Sales
Micro Center may have started asking some RTX 5090 buyers for ID and a signed declaration form. A Redditor on r/Microcenter says they bought a PowerSpec AI90 prebuilt with an RTX 5090 at the Tustin store, where a manager had them fill out a form and scan their driver's license. Apparently, staff called the process new, starting about two days earlier. The form looks to be an "Advanced Computing Product Purchaser Declaration" that asks for contact and ID details, and it reportedly says "No exports, No exceptions." The form requires buyers to certify that they will not export the hardware, nor will they resell to someone intending to take it outside the country. Micro Center hasn't officially commented on this incident or on the rule in general. 
The standard RTX 5090 isn't meant to be sold officially in China under US export rules, and MSI previously said that any units showing up there came through unauthorized parallel imports. That may be why the retailer wants a paper trail, but that's unconfirmed for now. Pricing could also play a role. NVIDIA has hiked RTX 5090 prices multiple times over the past few months, and German listings recently passed €5,000, about 73% above January. AI firms are reportedly buying RTX 5090 cards in bulk, tightening supply for consumers. If other stores follow Micro Center's approach, buying a 5090 in person could come with some paperwork. Regardless, we don't yet know whether this is a new widespread policy or a one-off.
Sources:

articles.title: 'Lanterns' dazzling season 1 viewership and season 2 writers room update rumor means I'm no longer afraid that HBO's Green Lantern TV show will be canceled
articles.text:
- Lanterns' weekly viewing figures have been revealed
- On average, 19 million people have tuned in to each episode on HBO and HBO Max worldwide
- A rumored writers' room update also suggests a season 2 renewal could be imminent
Lanterns is truly shining on the world stage.
According to audience measurement experts Nielsen (via Variety), HBO's Green Lantern TV show has been a huge hit with viewers across the globe. Indeed, per Nielsen's internal data, each episode of the sci-fi crime drama's first season has been watched by an average of 19 million people across HBO and its streaming sibling HBO Max. Of that figure, 12 million are in the US alone.
Impressive numbers though they are, Lanterns' global viewership is arguably even bigger than what Nielsen has reported. Indeed, because HBO and HBO Max aren't available in some world regions, Lanterns is also available on other streaming platforms. The chances are, then, that its audience share is even greater than we realize.
To put an even bigger spotlight on its stunning performance, Lanterns' debut season has, on average, drawn in more viewers per episode than The Pitt season 2. Considering how popular the aforementioned multi-award-winning medical drama is, it's to Lanterns' credit that it's outperforming The Pitt's most recent outing.
Given its success, it's more likely than ever that Lanterns will get a second season on HBO and some of the world's best streaming services, right? As a huge fan of the Aaron Pierre- and Kyle Chandler-fronted program, I certainly hope so.
I'll readily admit I feared the worst for Lanterns season 2 after comments made by HBO boss Casey Bloys in mid-September. However, with Lanterns posting nearly 20 million average views per chapter, and DC Studios co-head James Gunn confirming (via Threads) that its eighth episode is only its debut season's finale, rather than a series finale, I'm starting to convince myself that it's a matter of when, not if, the DC Universe (DCU) TV show will get another run.
That growing confidence is helped by recent speculation that a full writers' room has been assembled to thrash out a potential plot for the DCU Chapter One show's sophomore season.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
As reported by Nexus Point News, five writers have joined showrunner and co-creator Chris Mundy to come up with a compelling storyline for another season.
Vanessa Baden Kelly, who penned two of this season's eight entries, has returned, while new faces in Chris Cantwell, Nakkiah Lui, Zack Whedon, and Selwyn Seyfu Hinds have also come on board.
I should point out that the assembly of a writers' room doesn't guarantee that Lanterns season 2 has been greenlit internally. It's still possible, then, that Gunn, Mundy, and company won't move ahead with what I'd expect to be another eight-part installment.
Still, there's clearly an appetite from Lanterns' cast and crew, as well as its growing audience, for another season. Let's collectively hope that this season's finale, which airs Sunday (October 4) in the Americas and Monday (October 5) everywhere else, ends with confirmation that season 2 is officially in development.

articles.title: Cette appli contourne les restrictions de Microsoft pour installer Windows 11 26H2 sur les très vieux PC
articles.text:
Installer Windows 11 sur un très vieux PC non compatible avec Windows 11 n’est sans doute pas la meilleure des idées si l’on souhaite profiter du système d’exploitation de Microsoft sans quelques lenteurs. C’est sans doute la raison pour laquelle Microsoft oblige la prise en charge des instructions processeur SSE4.2 et PopCnt depuis Windows 11 24H2.
Sans celles-ci, les machines équipées d’un processeur ne prenant pas en charge ces instructions sont en principe incapables d’installer ou de démarrer Windows. Un développeur a pourtant trouvé une parade et a développé un utilitaire capable de contourner les restrictions mises en place par Microsoft.
POP4.2 installe Windows 11 sur les très vieux PC
Après avoir analysé le code assembleur du noyau de Windows, un développeur indépendant a pu créer un utilitaire capable de contourner les restrictions mises en place par Microsoft sur les versions 24H2, 25H2 et 26H2 de Windows 11.
En principe, le système d’exploitation de Microsoft vérifie en effet la présence de SSE4.2, une instruction dont la majorité des fichiers de l’OS n’a pas réellement besoin. En modifiant un octet spécifique dans le noyau 26100.7171 de Windows, POP4.2, c’est le nom de l’outil développé par Smu1zel, permet de forcer Windows 11 à ignorer cette vérification matérielle.
Concrètement, l’utilitaire permet de faire fonctionner Windows 11 sur les processeurs ne disposant pas du jeu d’instruction SSE4.2, mais prenant tout de même en charge PopCnt. Pour s’assurer du bon fonctionnement de son outil, le développeur a testé celui-ci, avec succès, sur un PC de 2008 équipé d’un processeur quad-core AMD Phenom X4 9600.
L’utilitaire POP4.2, gratuit et open source, est téléchargeable sur le dépôt Github officiel où toute la marche à suivre pour l’utiliser est décrite.
Si le programme est fonctionnel, il n’est pas parfait et conserve toujours quelques limitations matérielles. Son développeur explique, entre autres, que certains systèmes équipés de Chipsets Nvidia nForce peuvent freezer. L’outil reste par ailleurs incompatible avec les machines animées par les processeurs Intel Core 2, ces derniers ne prenant pas en charge l’instruction SSE4a dans laquelle se trouve l’instruction PopCnt.

articles.title: PS5 estrena escalado por IA: Sony lanza QSSR, su solución para que el modelo base aguante el tipo unos años más
articles.text:
Sony va a llevar el escalado por machine learning a la PS5 estándar. La tecnología se llama Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) y es una versión más ligera del PSSR que, hasta ahora, solo podía ejecutar la PS5 Pro. Dos juegos, Marvel's Wolverine y Ghost of Yōtei, han recibido un parche para ofrecer esta tecnología como una opción gráfica adicional. Te contamos todos los detalles.
Una PS5 base que tiene que durar. El principal argumento de venta de la PS5 Pro ha sido una mejor calidad de imagen a través del escalado por IA, y QSSR parece que traslada ahora esta misma idea a la PS5 base. Muchos juegos de esta generación se renderizan a resoluciones internas bajas y dependen de un escalado básico para alcanzar una resolución 4K, lo que a menudo hace que las imágenes no sean todo lo nítidas que nos gustaría o se noten artefactos que corrompan un poco la imagen.
Desde Digital Foundry se han pasado varias probando QSSR, y afirman que podría marcar una diferencia real en esos casos. Y no solo eso, pues hay que tener en cuenta que con la crisis de componentes que afecta a toda la cadena de suministro tecnológica, aumentando el coste del hardware como consecuencia, puede ser un balón de oxígeno para la PS5 estándar para que aguante el tipo unos cuantos años más.
En detalle. Sony afirma que QSSR proviene del Project Amethyst, una colaboración que tiene con la empresa AMD para el renderizado de gráficos por IA, y se apoya en dos elementos: una red neuronal reducida y una implementación ajustada y optimizada para el hardware de PS5. La compañía sigue considerando el PSSR como el jamón de pata negra del escalado en su consola, mientras que QSSR se presenta más como una alternativa más económica.
Según Daniel Craig, ingeniero de gráficos de Sony, la PS5 Pro cuenta con 300 TOPS (unidad que cuantifica cuántos billones de operaciones matemáticas puede realizar un procesador en un solo segundo) de hardware dedicado a IA. La PS5 base no tiene ninguno, por lo que QSSR se apoya principalmente en cálculos matemáticos en FP16 (formato en coma flotante de 16 bits) y una serie de trucos de eficiencia, incluyendo un uso intensivo de instrucciones matemáticas empaquetadas (packed math).
Pruebas. Según cuentan desde Digital Foundry, QSSR mejora la estabilidad temporal y el detalle fino, gestiona mejor los elementos diminutos y produce menos artefactos en elementos como el follaje en movimiento. El medio señala que las mejoras fueron más visibles en Marvel's Wolverine, ya que en Ghost of Yōtei, que ya se veía bastante bien de base, fueron menores.
Afecta al rendimiento. En Wolverine, Digital Foundry midió QSSR en aproximadamente entre 1,5 y 1,8 milisegundos por fotograma al escalar de 864p a 1440p. Con la tasa de fotogramas sin limitar, eso significa entre 8 y 10 fotogramas por segundo menos que con el propio escalador del juego. En el modo rendimiento a 60 Hz la brecha se reduce, ya que la resolución dinámica disminuye la resolución interna para compensar. Apuntar a 4K parece que ya se va bastante, situándose en torno a los 4,4 milisegundos.
En el modo rendimiento de Ghost of Yōtei, el medio descubrió que QSSR funcionaba casi a la misma velocidad que la implementación existente de FSR 3 del juego, pero claro al haber solamente dos juegos que sean compatibles con esta tecnología, habrá que esperar para que esta solución alternativa se vaya expandiendo a más juegos para ver cómo evoluciona.
No llega al nivel de PS5 Pro. Lógicamente, por pura capacidad de hardware, el remedio no llega al nivel de PSSR. El propio Craig contaba a Digital Foundry que los equipos de PS5 deben ser más flexibles que en Pro, ajustando las resoluciones de salida interna, intermedia y final para cada modo gráfico. Los resultados de Digital Foundry sugieren que 1440p es el objetivo natural para QSSR, y no el 4K.
Qué viene ahora. Que QSSR se extienda depende de los desarrolladores. Sony dice que estará disponible para todos los estudios de PlayStation, y Craig lo describe como un “reemplazo directo” para los juegos que ya admiten PSSR, necesitando solo unos pocos días de ajuste. También afirma que añadirlo a los juegos existentes es relativamente fácil y tiene poco riesgo. Igual esta tecnología le viene bien a la PS5 base con Grand Theft Auto VI, aunque esta decisión depende enteramente de Rockstar.

articles.title: Buying an RTX 5090 from Micro Center now means signing a form promising it won't leave the US
articles.text:
WTF?! It seems that if you have the money to buy a pre-built RTX 5090 PC from Micro Center, and there's one in stock, you'll also have to sign a declaration promising not to export the flagship graphics card. It's unclear exactly how enforceable this form is, though, and whether it would actually stop people who are selling the chips to China and elsewhere.
Redditor Krothic writes that they recently bought a PowerSpec Ai90 prebuilt PC packing an RTX 5090. The store manager informed them that buying the PC required that they fill in a form and have their drivers license scanned, connecting their name to their purchase.
After the section requiring details such as name, photo ID, and phone number, the form states that the person must be buying the PC for their own personal or business use in the US, "or I have accurately identified the actual end user above."
The next point specifies that the product will remain in the United States, and will not be exported, reexported, transferred, resold, supplied, or anything else that causes the PC to leave the US to any destination, for any reason.
These days, getting hold of an RTX 5090 usually means handing over more than $7,000, with at least one special edition model priced at $11,229. In many cases, it's cheaper to buy an entire pre-built PC featuring the GPU than to buy the card individually – and you obviously get all the other components as part of the price.
With its 32GB of VRAM, the RTX 5090 is considered as much of an AI-focused card as a gaming one, if not more so. As such, the standard RTX 5090 is restricted from export to mainland China under US export controls; Nvidia made separate 5090 D and 5090 D V2 versions for the Chinese market.
The Micro Center manager said the process had been in place for the past two days. There are certainly a lot of questions surrounding it. What if the buyer decides to sell the system or its GPU second-hand years later and that person then sells it overseas? What if the system is stolen and ends up abroad?
One comment on the thread also claims that Micro Center also won't sell an RTX 5090 to a customer if they've ever bought one in the past. Another user said the same thing happened to them.
Ultimately, this all feels like another reason why people aren't going to want to buy an RTX 5090, or a system containing one, right now. And, once again, it's AI's fault.

articles.title: Judge dismisses antitrust lawsuits over Google AI Overviews
articles.text:
Google has won a dismissal of two lawsuits alleging that the company’s AI Overviews in Search negatively impact internet traffic.
Last year, news publisher Penske Media Corporation (PMC) and ed tech company Chegg filed antitrust lawsuits against Google, arguing that the search giant’s AI Overviews were drawing people away from their sites. Google naturally filed to dismiss the suits, and on Oct. 1, U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta ultimately ruled in favour of Google.
In court, Mehta said AI Overviews don’t violate antitrust law as neither Penske nor Chegg had formal agreements with Google.
“Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free,” wrote Mehta. “But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works.”
That said, Mehta, who was the same judge who ruled in 2024 that Google operates a search monopoly, did acknowledge that Google’s AI search features is harming publishers.
“The court does not treat Plaintiffs’ alleged harms lightly,” he wrote. “Nor is it unsympathetic to the situation publishers now find themselves in, and the knock-on consequences to journalists, educators, and other online creators whose content Google takes and repurposes without compensation.”
Indeed, there has been a lot of research from groups like the Pew Research Institute that demonstrates that AI Overviews can siphon as much as 50 per cent — if not more — of traffic from websites. That’s to say nothing of the misinformation that AI Overviews continues to spread. But of course, Mehta’s job was simply to determine whether Google’s harmful AI tools actually broke any laws, and ultimately, he concluded that wasn’t the case.
Image credit: Google
Source: United States District Court Via: Engadget

articles.title: OpenAI warnt über 100 Organisationen wegen KI-Angriffen: Wie sie die Vorfälle aufgespürt haben
articles.text:
Nach Untersuchungen: OpenAI warnt über 100 Organisationen vor eigenmächtigen KI-Agenten
Immer mehr Fälle werden bekannt, in denen KI-Agenten aus ihrer Sandbox-Umgebung ausgebrochen sind und Dritte über das Internet angegriffen haben. OpenAI hat erst kürzlich wegen eines weiteren Vorfalls das KI-Training fortgeschrittener Modelle gestoppt. Während der Untersuchungen vergangener Vorfälle sind jetzt noch mehr mögliche Verstöße von KI‑Agenten zutage gefördert worden, die andere Unternehmen als Ziel hatten.
Warum OpenAI andere vor KI-Agenten warnt
Das geht aus einem ausführlichen Bericht von OpenAI hervor, der sich mit der Aufarbeitung des Hugging-Face-Vorfalls und den daraus gezogenen Maßnahmen beschäftigt. Darin heißt es, dass das Unternehmen aktuell 50 Petabyte an Daten durchforstet, um den Vorfall allumfassend aufzuarbeiten. Dabei gehen die Verantwortlichen die Daten Monat für Monat durch und lassen sich auch von einer KI dabei helfen.
Die KI, die OpenAI hilft, sei in der Lage „diese Aufzeichnungen schneller als jede händische Untersuchung“ auszuwerten. Um diese Aufgabe stemmen zu können, setzt OpenAI 7.000 GB200- und GB300-GPUs ein, die täglich Kosten in Höhe von einer halben Million US-Dollar verschlingen sollen. Künftig will OpenAI die Computing-Power auch noch weiter erhöhen, um den Prozess zu verbessern.
Bei den Untersuchungen zeigte sich, dass über 100 Organisationen und Unternehmen zum Ziel von OpenAIs KI-Agenten geworden sind. Sämtliche Betroffenen wurden mittlerweile darüber informiert. OpenAI betont, dass diese Vorfälle die eigenen Kriterien von Cybersecurity-Zwischenfällen erfüllen, aber das nicht zwangsläufig bedeutet, dass auf sensible Informationen zugegriffen oder fremde Systeme gehackt werden konnten. Welche Unternehmen betroffen sind oder welche genauen Aktionen die KI-Agenten vorgenommen haben, lässt OpenAI dabei allerdings offen.
Abschließend betont das Unternehmen, dass wohl im Laufe der Untersuchungen noch weitere Fälle gefunden werden könnten. Gerade die „historischen Aktivitäten“ könnten dafür sorgen, dass OpenAI noch weitere Dritte über Angriffe informieren muss. Dabei verspricht das Unternehmen, klarzumachen, welche Aktivitäten passiert sind, wann sie gefunden wurden und was noch ungeklärt bleibt.

articles.title: US military ends long-running program to spot nuclear missile launches
articles.text:
In late 1970, a Titan IIIC rocket launched from Space Launch Complex 40 at what was then called Cape Canaveral Air Force Station. It carried a top-secret payload for the US military.
Much has changed in spaceflight since then. The Titan IIIC would bow out in 1982 after dozens of launches. Various Titans continued launching from Space Launch Complex 40 until 2005, at which point the US Air Force—in a competitive process hotly opposed by United Launch Alliance—turned the pad over to a small, largely unknown startup called SpaceX. And Cape Canaveral is now a “Space Force” station.
But those unspecified payloads? Until last month, some of them were still flying operationally.
They were looking for missile launches
The US government would later disclose that the top-secret payload that launched in November 1970 was a “Defense Support Program” satellite. The initial block of these satellites, launched from 1970 to 1973, had a mass of about 1 metric ton, and each carried about 2,000 infrared detectors. They were essentially very sensitive telescopes, and each satellite was launched into geosynchronous orbit.
For a time, these were among the most important satellites flown by the US, as they served to detect the launch of a nuclear warhead at the country. As a result, the Defense Support Program would become one of the primary elements of American military space power during the Cold War.
These initial satellites transformed experimental infrared observations into an operational program that continuously monitored the globe for missile launches. Initially built to identify Soviet ICBMs, they were essential for nuclear deterrence; later, they also became useful in conventional warfare, such as detecting Iraqi Scud missile launches.
Over time, the military added to the constellation, improving reliability and expanding their capabilities. Each satellite ended up having more than 6,000 infrared detectors and a mass of about 2.5 tons. Satellites in the Defense Support Program kept on flying into space until 2007. One of them, DSP-16, even launched on a space shuttle (Atlantis) in 1991.

articles.title: Why CISOs Struggle to Answer the Board's Three Hardest Questions, and How to Fix the Report
articles.text:
The quarterly board meeting is two weeks out. The security team is pulling exports from the identity provider, the cloud posture tool, the vulnerability scanner, the SIEM and the EDR console. Someone is building a spreadsheet to reconcile them. Someone else is turning that spreadsheet into slides.
Then a board member asks three questions:
- How secure is the organization, overall?
- What is the actual financial exposure?
- Is the security posture better than it was last quarter?
Most security leaders cannot answer any of them with confidence. Not because the data doesn't exist, but because it lives in a dozen tools that don't share context. A new guide to confident board reporting for CISOs takes on exactly this problem. This article walks through why traditional reporting fails and what a better model looks like.
Boards Have Stopped Trusting Activity Metrics
For years, security reporting has run on counts. Vulnerabilities found. Patches applied. Alerts closed. Phishing simulations passed. These numbers measure effort. They don't measure risk.
A board member hearing that the team closed thousands of findings last quarter has no way to judge whether the company is safer. The obvious follow-up, "safer from what, and by how much?", rarely has an answer.
Boards want three things:
- Exposure, not activity. Which business-critical assets could an attacker actually reach today?
- Trend, not snapshot. Is that exposure shrinking quarter over quarter?
- Money, not CVEs. What is the financial impact if those paths are used?
The Real Problem Lives in the Gaps Between Tools
The typical mid-size or growth enterprise runs an identity provider, a CSPM or CNAPP, endpoint detection, a SIEM, a vulnerability scanner and a long tail of SaaS applications. Each tool is accurate about its own slice. None of them sees how the slices connect. Attackers don't care about those boundaries.
Consider a realistic path:
- A contractor account in the identity provider still holds a group membership from a finished project. The identity tool rates it low risk.
- That group grants access to a SaaS app with an OAuth integration into the cloud environment. The SaaS security tool sees a normal integration.
- The integration runs under a service account with broad storage permissions. The cloud posture tool flags it as medium.
- That storage holds customer records. The data classification tool knows it's sensitive, but not who can reach it.
Four findings. Four tools. Four moderate scores. Together they form a critical path from a phishable account to the company's most sensitive data. No single dashboard shows it, so it doesn't make the board report. It gets found during an incident instead.
AI adoption widens this gap. AI agents, non-human identities, service accounts and MCP-connected tools are being added faster than anyone inventories them. Each one is a new identity with its own access, and most stacks were never designed to map where that access leads. Shadow AI becomes another set of unseen paths.
Why Adding Another Tool Doesn't Fix It
The reflex is to buy something that covers the gap. That usually produces one more console, one more export and one more column in the reconciliation spreadsheet.
The common pushback is fair: "We already have CSPM. We already have a Zero Trust architecture." Those investments matter. But they are controls, each scoped to a domain. The question the board is asking crosses domains. What's missing isn't another control. It's shared context between the controls already deployed.
This is the idea behind Cybersecurity Mesh Architecture (CSMA), a model Gartner describes for connecting distributed security tools through a common intelligence layer. Instead of replacing tools, CSMA correlates their data so identities, access, assets and exposures can be read as one graph. The CISO board reporting guide breaks down how this approach maps directly to the questions boards ask.
A Practical Framework for Board-Ready Reporting
Security leaders rebuilding their board report around exposure can follow a sequence like this:
1. Define the crown jewels with the business
Start with the assets whose compromise would hurt the business most: customer data stores, payment systems, PHI, source code, production infrastructure. Agree on them with business owners, not just the security team. This list anchors everything that follows.
2. Connect what is already deployed
Pull identity, cloud, endpoint, SaaS and vulnerability data into one correlated view. The goal is deduplication and enrichment, not new sensors. Agentless, API-based integration keeps deployment fast and avoids disrupting production.
3. Map real attack paths to those assets
Replace finding lists with paths. For each crown jewel, show which identities, human and non-human, can reach it, and through what chain of access and misconfiguration.
4. Prioritize by blast radius
A medium-severity misconfiguration on a path to customer data outranks a critical CVE on an isolated test server. Rank remediation by what it cuts off, not by its standalone score.
5. Translate exposure into financial terms
Tie each reachable crown jewel to a business impact estimate built with finance and risk teams. The report moves from "number of vulnerabilities" to "dollars at risk," which is the language boards already use for every other risk category.
6. Report the trend
Show how many attack paths to critical assets existed last quarter, how many exist now, and which remediation work closed them. This also answers the ROI question directly: it shows what the existing security stack is actually protecting.
What Changes in the Boardroom
When the report is built on attack paths instead of activity counts, the three hard questions get concrete answers:
- How secure are we? Here are the remaining paths to our most critical assets.
- What is our financial exposure? Here is the estimated impact if those paths are used.
- Are we improving? Here is how many paths were eliminated since last quarter, and what closed them.
That shifts the CISO's role in the meeting from defending spend to reporting measurable risk reduction. It also gives the security team a prioritized work queue that matches what leadership cares about.
Getting Started
Mesh is the unified intelligence layer for enterprise security teams operating across fragmented security stacks with no shared context. Connecting agentlessly to your existing tools, Mesh correlates signals across identity, cloud, SaaS, endpoint, and AI environments to reveal viable attack paths to your most critical assets. By providing enterprise-wide context that no individual tool can deliver alone, Mesh helps security teams prioritize what matters most and eliminate risk faster through guided workflows. Security leaders preparing for their next board cycle can download the CISO's Guide to Confident Board Reporting.

articles.title: Après Apple, c'est au tour de Rowenta de lancer son Vision Pro
articles.text:
Après Apple, c'est au tour de Rowenta de lancer son Vision Pro
Rowenta dévoile le X-Clean Vision Pro, un aspirateur laveur deux-en-un conçu pour aspirer et nettoyer les sols en un seul passage. L'appareil intègre un système d'assistance intelligente et une tête articulée pour faciliter le ménage quotidien.
Rowenta X-Clean Vision Pro
Le fabricant Rowenta serait-il un fan absolu d'Apple ? On pourrait le croire quand on sait que son prochain laveur de sol porte un nom qui parlera forcément aux aficionados de réalité virtuelle et de la marque à la pomme : le X-Clean Vision Pro. La firme de Vernon n'a pas soudainement décidé de se lancer dans la production de casques de réalité virtuelle puisque le X-Clean Vision Pro n'est qu'un "simple" nettoyeur de sol, dans la lignée du X-Clean 12. Comme ses illustres prédécesseurs (nous parlons toujours de nettoyeurs de sols, pas de casque RV), l'appareil combine l'aspiration et le lavage des sols en une seule étape. Ce modèle 2-en-1 vise à prendre en charge aussi bien la poussière que les taches humides ou les liquides renversés grâce à une motorisation dédiée et un système d'auto-propulsion réduisant le poids ressenti à 1 kg en main, une fonctionnalité déjà croisée sur le Roborock F25 Steam.
Des caractéristiques techniques pensées pour l'efficacité
Sur le plan technique, on ne retrouve aucun écran micro-OLED ni aucune puce M2 avec un CPU à 8 cœurs et encore moins de GPU à 10 cœurs dans le Rowenta X-Clean Vision Pro, mais il affiche une puissance d'aspiration de 20 kPa couplée à un rouleau rotatif atteignant 530 rotations par minute. Le casque de VR d'Apple peut-il en dire autant ? La brosse est configurée pour effectuer un nettoyage sur trois bords afin de traiter les angles et les bas de murs. Côté ergonomie, la machine s'appuie sur la technologie 180° Flex, un manche conçu pour se glisser sous les meubles bas jusqu'à une hauteur de 14 cm, mais qui n'est pas articulé comme le sont pourtant ceux des aspirateurs-balais X-Force Flex de la marque.
L'autonomie annoncée atteint jusqu'à 60 minutes en fonctionnement, avec un temps de charge complète estimé à 3 heures et 30 minutes. La gestion des fluides repose sur un système à double réservoir séparant l'eau propre de l'eau sale. Le réservoir de liquide propre présente une contenance de 800 ml, tandis que le bac de récupération d'eau usée affiche un volume de 620 ml.
Un suivi intelligent et une maintenance automatisée
Le fonctionnement repose également sur l'intégration du système Vision Detect Pro, qui éclaire les saletés pour les rendre plus visibles et adapte le lavage au niveau de souillure détecté. L'appareil propose quatre modes de nettoyage distincts : un mode Auto régulant le travail en fonction de la saleté, un mode Eco pour maximiser l'autonomie, un mode Max pour les surfaces très encrassées, ainsi qu'un mode d'aspiration des liquides.
Pour informer l'utilisateur, l'aspirateur dispose d'un écran LCD intelligent affichant des animations 3D ainsi que d'un système d'assistance vocale configuré en 22 langues : à nous les joies des corvées ménagères dans la langue de Dostoïevski ! À l'issue du nettoyage, le X-Clean Vision Pro prend en charge son propre entretien via une fonction d'auto-nettoyage du rouleau suivie d'une phase de séchage automatique, limitant ainsi les interventions manuelles.
Le X-Clean Vision Pro sera disponible dans le courant du mois d'octobre et il sera bien plus simple de se le procurer que son auguste homonyme : il en coûtera 550 €, soit sept fois moins que le "regretté" Apple Vision Pro.

articles.title: How I kept cool with NYC's free battery program for window AC units
articles.text:
My family has spent four summers participating in demand response programs whereby utility companies pay customers to reduce energy use on the hottest summer days. Most summers have involved carefully precooling our New York City apartment before switching off the air conditioners and sweating it out during the designated demand response periods.
But this year, we kept our window air conditioners running throughout a heat dome event that drove daytime temperatures into the triple digits and made the nights oppressively hot. The difference was that we powered the air conditioners through two household batteries tucked away unobtrusively in the corners of our living room and bedroom.
We were among about 1,000 New York City households that took part in a free and growing program offered by the local startup Every Electric. The company’s proposition is simple: Get one or more batteries delivered to your home, plug the batteries into a standard wall electrical outlet, and then plug your window air conditioners into the batteries. Households can keep running air conditioners as usual during peak demand periods while also earning money through the local demand response program with the utility company Con Edison.
“Being able to make air conditioners drop off the grid without actually impacting the comfort of residents was really awesome to see,” said Andrew Wang, co-founder and CEO of Every Electric, in an interview with Ars.
Wang and cofounder Richard May first met while working together as postdoctoral researchers at the Columbia Electrochemical Energy Center at Columbia University in New York City. In 2023, they launched the startup under the name Standard Potential Co., with a focus on developing sodium-ion battery chemistry for commercialization.
But they soon pivoted to a very different business plan—deploying residential batteries across New York City households to create a network of energy storage resources acting as a virtual power plant. The company officially rebranded as Every Electric in 2026.
