articles.title: Dia das Crianças: Nintendo Switch 2 surge em oferta na Amazon • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Dia das Crianças: Nintendo Switch 2 surge em oferta na Amazon
Nintendo Switch 2 com tela ampla em Full HD e bateria de longa duração recebe 16% de desconto; console portátil é opção de presente para crianças
O Nintendo Switch 2 entrou em oferta por R$ 3.799 no Pix na Amazon. O mais recente videogame da Nintendo com tela de 120 Hz e recursos de Ray Tracing, lançado por R$ 4.499, fica 16% mais barato e se torna a melhor opção para quem deseja comprá-lo parcelado para o Dia das Crianças.
O Nintendo Switch 2 tem uma ampla tela LCD de 7,9 polegadas com resolução Full HD e taxa de atualização de 120 Hz no Modo Portátil. Quem prefere se divertir em telas maiores, o console pode ser conectado à TV via dock e reproduzir jogos com qualidade até 4K.
O videogame adota o chipset Nvidia T239 e 12 GB de RAM, somando forças para executar jogos com efeitos de luz e sombra realistas com as tecnologias DLSS e Ray Tracing. Os 256 GB de armazenamento interno entregam um espaço equilibrado, mas os jogadores mais “hardcore” podem expandir a memória com cartões microSD de até 2 TB.
A autonomia do Nintendo Switch 2 gira em torno de 6,5 horas, sendo ideal para viagens ou para evitar o “doomscrolling” em casa. Vale dizer que o console permite jogar no modo semiportátil, desacoplando os novos controles Joy-Cons 2 para jogar em dupla em qualquer lugar.
Os Joy-Cons 2 continuam oferecendo opções de controle de movimento, além de trazer novos recursos de jogabilidade. Por exemplo, é possível transformá-los em mouse para melhores experiências com jogos de estratégia em tempo real (RTS) e de tiro em primeira pessoa (FPS).
O console da Nintendo tem conexão Wi-Fi 6, permitindo tanto jogar partidas online quanto acessar a loja virtual Nintendo eShop para baixar e comprar jogos digitais. Para quem quer uma experiência imersiva, ele possui Bluetooth 5.2 para conectar fones de ouvido sem fio.
Por fim, o Nintendo Switch 2 (R$ 3.799 no Pix) é retrocompatível com quase todos os títulos do Switch original. Então, você pode levar a biblioteca do antigo videogame para o novo e, em alguns casos, experimentar os jogos com melhores gráficos e desempenho.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Copenhagen's Good Tape raises €600k and becomes independent from Zetland; Zendesk co-founder joins board | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Good Tape, the Copenhagen-based AI transcription company, has raised €600k from Nordic Makers, an investment group founded by former unicorn founders that invests its own capital in early-stage Nordic startups, with an average ticket size of €500k.
Zendesk co-founder Alexander Aghassipour led the investment for Nordic Makers and has joined Good Tape’s board. Good Tape also announced that this round is part of a management buy-out in which the founders took over Zetland’s ownership stake, the Danish media outlet that incubated the startup. This makes Good Tape an independent company.
“There is so much uncertainty and scepticism around AI tools right now, that many people are getting too overwhelmed to use them effectively. We need to give people products that they don’t have to worry about, that still leverage the power of AI. Like being able to search and interact intelligently with years worth of interviews, in the way Explore allows,” said Aghassipour, co-founder of Zendesk and partner, Nordic Makers.
Founded in 2022, Good Tape began life as an internal tool at Zetland, the Danish member-funded newsroom, before spinning out as a standalone business. It was founded by journalists who needed accurate transcripts without handing over sensitive information to outside vendors.
It transforms spoken audio into usable text while keeping full control of customer data, holds ISO 27001 certification, is GDPR-compliant, stores data in the EU, and does not train AI models on customer material. Since spinning out, Good Tape has completed more than 15 million transcriptions in over 100 languages for journalists, researchers, lawyers, consultants, and public-sector teams.
The company says it is now used by 3 million people across more than 150 countries. With the buyout, co-founders Ýmir Gyðuson Gíslason and Lasse Finderup take control of Zetland’s stake in the company.
“Good Tape was built inside a newsroom by people who needed to trust where their interviews ended up. Zetland gave us the room to build it, and we owe them a lot. Now we’re going all in on that trust. With Explore, Good Tape goes from transcribing your interviews to also connecting them, and it’s still safe for your most sensitive material,” said Finderup, co-founder and CEO, Good Tape.
Alongside the ownership change, the company has launched Good Tape Explore, a new feature that links a user’s recordings together to surface patterns across past interviews. The new Explore feature connects each new recording to a user’s full transcription history, surfacing contradictions, shifting positions, and supporting arguments, with every insight linked back to the original recording.
Good Tape says the Explore tool will let journalists, researchers and teams trace what a source said and when, follow how their positions evolve across multiple recordings, while being within the same private, EU-hosted workspace.

articles.title: Fine-tune a search agent with multi-turn RL on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Fine-tune a search agent with multi-turn RL on Amazon SageMaker AI
Search agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are transforming how enterprises retrieve information. Rather than requiring users to craft the perfect query, a search agent autonomously decides what to search for, which retrieval strategy to use, and when to stop searching. It does this across multiple rounds of interaction, refining its approach based on what it has already retrieved.
However, getting this multi-step behavior to work well is hard. No base model arrives knowing your tools or your environment. Prompt a small model and you rarely get dependable multi-turn behavior. Prompt a frontier model and it often works, but you pay for that capability in latency and cost. Fine-tuning offers a third path: you teach a small model your tools and environment directly. The result is a small model’s speed and cost with the reliability that would otherwise require a frontier model.
Even though fine-tuning is the natural next step, the traditional approaches each fall short. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) depends on expert demonstrations of ideal multi-turn trajectories, which are costly to collect and usually don’t exist for your setup. Single-turn reinforcement learning (RL), such as RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR), scores one response at a time. But a search agent makes interdependent decisions across many turns, each one building on the context before it. Optimizing a single step in isolation misses those dependencies entirely.
What you need is a training approach that optimizes the agent across the full multi-turn trajectory. The reward signal only needs to reflect whether the final outcome was good. That is exactly what multi-turn reinforcement learning (MTRL) provides. It trains the agent to make good decisions across a full sequence of steps, bakes in your environment-specific behavior, and gives you control over output quality. Because you run a smaller, specialized model, you also get faster, cheaper inference.
In this post, we describe how we fine-tuned a search agent using Amazon SageMaker AI multi-turn reinforcement learning (MTRL) and share the results we observed in retrieval quality and reliability. We begin by explaining what Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL is and how it works.
What is Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL?
With Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL, you can fine-tune LLMs using reinforcement learning in multi-turn interaction settings. It frames an agentic task as a sequence of decisions, uses multi-turn rollouts to generate training data, and optimizes the model with policy gradient algorithms.
Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL offers:
- Modular agent-environment interface: You keep integration low-code. You define custom rewards, custom tool loops, and multi-turn conversation shapes.
- Serverless execution: You get production-scale agentic RL at per-token pricing without provisioning or managing GPU clusters.
- Asynchronous rollout and trajectory collection: You run generation and gradient updates in parallel with bounded off-policy staleness, so training stays fast without drifting too far from the current policy.
- A native algorithm library: You choose from Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Clipped Importance Sampling Policy Optimization (CISPO), and importance-sampling (IS) losses, paired with group-based advantage estimators (GRPO, GRPO pass@k, RLOO, and more).
- Resumable training: You can split long training runs across multiple jobs to work beyond single-job time limits.
- Trajectory and reward observability: You can inspect what your agent did turn by turn and across training steps in MLflow managed by Amazon SageMaker AI.
- Evaluation jobs: You can report reward, pass@k, and trajectory metrics before deploying to an Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint or Amazon Bedrock.
This makes MTRL a natural fit for search agents: you have a clear reward signal (retrieval quality), a multi-turn interaction loop (the agent issuing queries and receiving results), and a well-defined environment (the search tools).
Environment and setup
Our setup relied on the following:
- An AWS account with access to Amazon SageMaker AI in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region (us-west-2).
- Training and validation datasets uploaded to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) in the required format (see the MTRL documentation for details).
- A deployed agent endpoint that exposes BM25 and vector search tools for the MTRL environment to call during rollouts.
- Familiarity with Amazon SageMaker AI and Python.
Solution overview
In this post, we use Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL to fine-tune a Qwen3.6-27B model (supported in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2)) for a search agent. The search agent is an LLM-powered system that autonomously uses search tools to find, gather, and synthesize information to answer a question or complete a task.
We focus on an enterprise search setting where the agent has two tools available:
- Lexical search (BM25): Finds exact keyword matches by counting word frequencies. Best for queries with specific terms or identifiers.
- Vector search: Converts queries and documents into embedding vectors and computes similarities. This is recommended for semantic or conceptual queries.
We also limit the number of turns (one turn is one round of user-assistant interaction), preventing the agent from generating excessively long responses and encouraging efficient search behavior.
Training setup
This section walks through the three key components of our training setup: the datasets, the reward function, and the MTRL job configuration.
Datasets
We use the following datasets for training and testing:
| Dataset | Train/Test | Public Link | Description | 
| FRAMES | Train | HuggingFace | Multi-hop factoid QA requiring synthesis across multiple Wikipedia articles. | 
| BRIGHT | Train | HuggingFace | Reasoning-intensive retrieval across 12 domains, where relevance needs reasoning, not keyword overlap. | 
| Enterprise RAG | Train | GitHub | A benchmark of over 500,000 synthetic enterprise documents and 500 questions for training and evaluating RAG systems on internal company knowledge | 
| ESCI | Train | GitHub | A multilingual product-search dataset labeling query–product pairs as Exact, Substitute, Complement, or Irrelevant | 
| Musique | Train | GitHub | A question-answering dataset built by composing single-hop questions into challenging multi-hop reasoning problems. | 
| MLQA | Train | HuggingFace | A parallel extractive question-answering benchmark covering seven languages for evaluating cross-lingual comprehension. | 
| FreshStack | Test | HuggingFace | Recent developer-tech Q&A over Stack Overflow + docs for five topics. | 
| WixQA | Test | HuggingFace | Help-center support QA over the Wix knowledge base. | 
| BrowseComp-Plus | Test | GitHub | Hard deep-research queries over ~100K human-verified open-web documents. | 
| Wands | Test | HuggingFace | A Wayfair product-search dataset containing over 42,000 query–product relevance judgments labeled as Exact, Partial, or Irrelevant. | 
We preprocess the datasets into the format recognized by the MTRL service according to the documentation. We further reserve 5 percent of the training instances within each dataset as validation instances.
Reward function
Our main metric is nDCG@10 (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain at rank 10). nDCG@10 is a standard information retrieval metric that measures how well the top 10 retrieved documents match the ideal ranking. It rewards systems that place highly relevant documents near the top of the list, with a score of 1.0 meaning perfect ranking and 0.0 meaning no relevant documents retrieved. We use nDCG@10 directly as the reward function in MTRL. This is a trajectory-level reward where the agent completes its full multi-turn search, and the reward reflects how well the final retrieved documents match the ground truth.
When the agent reaches the maximum number of turns or the maximum sampling tokens in a single turn, we assign a reward of -1 to explicitly teach the model to avoid these failure modes. This kind of penalty-based reward design is effective at steering the model away from undesirable behavior without needing to hand-craft complex intermediate rewards.
MTRL job configuration
One of the appeals of Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL is how little you need to configure to get going. We change three hyperparameters and leave everything else at the default values. The following code snippet shows how to configure and launch the training job using the MultiTurnRLTrainer SDK:
The key hyperparameters we change are:
- max_epochs: 1 controls how many full passes over the training data.
- global_batch_size: 128 sets the number of prompts per training step.
- rollout_max_concurrency: 32 controls how many rollouts run in parallel during trajectory collection.
That’s the whole setup. The choices that usually demand RL expertise, the algorithm, the advantage estimator, the off-policy staleness bounds, all run on defaults. Getting from the base model to the results in the next section required nothing more than the preceding configuration.
Results
MTRL fine-tuning improved the search agent on three of four held-out benchmarks and made it substantially more reliable across all of them. The largest gains came on BrowseComp-Plus (+23.7 percent nDCG@10) and WixQA (+18.4 percent), with a smaller gain on Wands and a slight regression on FreshStack. The reliability improvement was the more striking result. On BrowseComp-Plus, the failure rate fell from 22.89 percent to 0.68 percent. This means the agent learned not only to search better but also to finish the task within its turn and token budget. The sections that follow walk through the training curves and the per-benchmark numbers.
Training progress
The following figure shows the reward (nDCG@10) on both training and validation instances over the course of training. The x-axis represents training steps and the y-axis shows the nDCG@10 score. Two lines track training and validation reward, both rising steadily before plateauing. MTRL training can span multiple days and the MTRL service has a default time limit of 24 hours, which is adjustable through the CreateJob JSON schema. If a job is stopped or has failed because of timeout or infrastructure error, you can continue training from a previous checkpoint with resume support.
The figure plots nDCG@10 against training steps for both training and validation sets. Both curves increase steadily as fine-tuning progresses and saturate by the end of training, suggesting further training would not be beneficial.
Test performance
The following table compares the fine-tuned model against the original Qwen3.6-27B on four held-out test datasets. All metrics in the table are computed from our evaluation runs on the datasets listed in the preceding section.
Column definitions:
- Size is the number of questions in the dataset.
- nDCG@10 is the standard Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain. The failed tasks are assigned nDCG@10 of 0.
- Failure rate is the percentage of questions where the agent hits an error (for example, exceeding the turn limit or token budget).
- Turns (avg) is the average number of turns per question.
| benchmark | size | model | ndcg@10 | fail_rate | turns | 
| WixQA | 400 | Qwen3.6-27B | 0.5725 | 0.67% | 4.3 | 
| WixQA | 400 | Qwen3.6-27B-finetune | 0.6781 | 0.17% | 4.5 | 
| Wands | 147 | Qwen3.6-27B | 0.5762 | 0.00% | 2.2 | 
| Wands | 147 | Qwen3.6-27B-finetune | 0.6112 | 0.00% | 2.9 | 
| FreshStack | 672 | Qwen3.6-27B | 0.4112 | 0.20% | 3.1 | 
| FreshStack | 672 | Qwen3.6-27B-finetune | 0.4089 | 0.05% | 2.8 | 
| BrowseComp-Plus | 830 | Qwen3.6-27B | 0.5136 | 22.89% | 7.0 | 
| BrowseComp-Plus | 830 | Qwen3.6-27B-finetune | 0.6354 | 0.68% | 6.3 | 
The results show that RL fine-tuning made a meaningful difference:
- Better search quality: As shown in the preceding table, nDCG@10 improved on WixQA (from 0.5725 to 0.6781, a +18.4 percent gain), on Wands (from 0.5762 to 0.6112, a +6 percent), and on BrowseComp-Plus (from 0.5136 to 0.6354, a +23.7 percent gain). The score decreased slightly on FreshStack.
- Fewer failures: Assigning a reward of -1 for failure cases was highly effective. On BrowseComp-Plus, the failure rate dropped from 22.89 percent to only 0.68 percent.
Clean up
If you do explore this approach, remember to clean up the resources afterward to avoid ongoing charges:
- Stop or delete the MTRL training job in the Amazon SageMaker AI console if it’s still running.
- Delete the model artifacts in Amazon S3 if they’re no longer needed.
- Delete any deployed endpoints that were created for evaluation.
Conclusion
In this post, we described our experience using Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL to fine-tune an LLM-powered search agent with reinforcement learning. With minimal configuration, the fine-tuned model showed substantial improvements in retrieval quality, failure rate, and turn efficiency (fewer turns per question).
Key takeaways from our experience with Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL:
- Low barrier to entry: Default configurations work well, and no deep RL expertise is required to get started.
- Serverless infrastructure: No need to provision GPUs or manage distributed training clusters. You pay per-token.
- Resumable training: Long training runs can be split across multiple jobs.
- Direct optimization: You train against your actual task metric rather than proxy losses.
- Full observability: You can inspect trajectories turn by turn in MLflow managed by Amazon SageMaker AI to understand what the agent learned.
Next steps
If you want to apply this approach to your own agents, here are some useful starting points:
- Consult the Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL documentation.
- Prepare your dataset in the required format.
- Prepare your agent and define your reward function based on your task-specific metric.
- Start with default configurations, which worked well in our experience.
- Evaluate and iterate.

articles.title: California bill requiring 3D printers to block firearm printing becomes law — existing machines are exempt, but mandate hinges on unwritten ASTM standard
articles.text:
California bill requiring 3D printers to block firearm printing becomes law — existing machines are exempt, but mandate hinges on unwritten ASTM standard
Assuming a standard is published, that is.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed into law a bill that requires 3D printer manufacturers to include firearm-blocking technology in their products once an industry standard is published by ASTM International. This makes California the second state to enact firearm restrictions on 3D printers following New York. Two other states, Colorado and Washington state, also have similar bills that would require “blocking features” moving through state legislatures.
Since the law only affects 3D printers that have yet to be sold, existing 3D printers do not need to be retrofitted with firearm-blocking technology, addressing one of the major concerns of the 3D printing community. It’s also not a straightforward ban on non-compliant printers and only regulates the sale and transfer of 3D printers, not their ownership or use.
The application of firearm-blocking technology on 3D printers will only be required for manufacturers once ASTM International, a non-profit organization that sets voluntary standards across different industries, publishes or adopts a standard for firearm-blocking technology for 3D printers. The law mandates the California Department of Justice (DOJ) to check for a standard quarterly, starting no later than July 1, 2027, until July 1, 2029. If the organization hasn’t published a standard by that date, then the DOJ is no longer required to check for it, meaning the process to write the guidelines or regulations that manufacturers need to follow to sell 3D printers in California might not even begin.
There are currently two primary ways to detect if a print file is intended for a 3D-printed firearm — it could either be matched against a known database of gun files or analyzed by a trained model to determine if the design could potentially be used for a firearm. However, both techniques suffer from shortcomings. The former could easily be defeated by just modifying the file, like changing its size or splitting it into multiple pieces for later assembly, while the latter is prone to false positives and could prevent the printing of barrels, brackets, levers, tubes, and other parts that may look similar but have a totally different, legitimate use. This is one of the reasons why the Electronic Frontier Foundation said in June 2026 that “there is no world where the mandated technology actually works as intended.”
The California law attempts to address these concerns raised by 3D printing enthusiasts by mandating the DOJ to base its implementation on standards set by ASTM International instead of defining it itself. So, until the standards group publishes or adopts one within the set timeframe, the requirements for manufacturers to build the technology into their 3D printer models would not come into play.

articles.title: Meta Muse has already broken a record: it beats all competitors in data collection, Surfshark warns
articles.text:
Meta Muse has already broken a record: it beats all competitors in data collection, Surfshark warns
Meta's newly launched AI agent is surpassed by its ‘older brother,’ Meta AI
- Muse is the most data-hungry chatbot, warns Surfshark
- It is surpassed only by Meta AI
- The VPN reiterates caution about entrusting your data to Big Tech
Meta’s Muse has been out for barely a month, yet it has already won the competition for the title of the most data-hungry chatbot.
The warning comes from Surfshark, one of the best VPNs, which recently conducted research ranking the most privacy-invasive AI chatbots. In its findings, Meta’s AI agent Muse, embodied by Jolly, the Labubu-style character that promises to execute tasks on your behalf, has already outperformed all its competitors when it comes to data harvesting.
Only another AI tool stands between Muse and the top spot: the older sibling, Meta AI, remains the undisputed data-harvesting front-runner.
Hungry for data
“Meta is unbeatable in data collection," stresses Surfshark. In its latest analysis, the VPN makes its case by comparing 13 widely used AI chatbots and the types of data they collect, as listed on the Apple App Store.
Indeed, Meta's Muse and Meta AI collect almost twice as many types of data as their competitors: 31 and 33 out of 35 types, respectively.
Next comes Google Gemini with 24 types. The trio uniquely collects highly sensitive information including ethnic data, sexual orientation, trade union, political opinion, genetic and biometric data.
ChatGPT comes fourth with 17 data types - a number that has alarmingly increased by 70 per cent since last year, with the chatbot now extending its data snatch to health and fitness, audio recordings and search history.
Gemini, Meta AI, Muse and Perplexity also capture location data, while ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Claude and Copilot retrieve approximate location information.
The winners of the ‘least intrusive’ title are Pi, Duck.ai and Mistral Vibe, with Pi remarkably collecting only user ID, product interaction and crash data.
NEW: Leave No Trace — A weekly newsletter on digital privacy and online surveillance.
Leave No Trace investigates the companies and governments putting our digital freedom at risk — and the people fighting back.
📩 Subscribe now to get every edition delivered to your inbox every Friday, launching this September.
My data to Meta? I’ll think about it
While Muse is marketed as a tool capable of understanding users’ objectives and pursuing them autonomously, Surfshark points out that the large-scale data collection practices employed by the agentic AI app represent a frightening concern for online privacy.
Indeed, Muse’s invasive nature enables it to collect an extraordinary amount of highly sensitive information from calendars, emails, and bank accounts. It then combines this with the contextual data gathered from the user’s interactions, thereby managing to draw up an exceptionally accurate profile of your digital identity.
This information can then be merged with other datasets for advertising or training purposes, leaving users with very little control over how their data is stored, sold, potentially leaked, or corrupted.
Indeed, a security researcher has already warned that Muse can be manipulated into sending your voice recordings to a hacker’s server. Users have also reported instances in which the tool allegedly read their personal messages without permission and then lied about it, as well as cases in which its severe execution faults backfired on users, exposing sensitive information.
And while there’s debate over whether Muse is genuinely useful for what it claims to offer or whether it truly helps users perform better rather than merely wasting their time, others describe growing unease at the prospect of giving the keys to their digital life to a company that never showed any remorse for monetising user data.
Indeed, Meta is currently also facing hefty fines ranging from $18 billion relating to addiction amongst minors, to €1.2 billion for the improper handling of user data in 2023. This is also the same company known for its ‘pervert glasses’, which can record people without their consent and which have sparked widespread controversy as they have reportedly been used for harassment and stalking.
Given all this, steering clear of this major data collector for a while longer might simply be a marvelous idea.
Better enforceability is needed
Additionally, while these fines may seem exorbitant, it is worrying that the financial impact of such punishments rarely acts as a deterrent to these large technology companies, whose market capitalisation runs into the hundreds of billions of dollars.
In its research, Proton previously found that the $7.8 billion in privacy and competition fines imposed on Big Tech in 2025 could be collectively paid by these firms in less than a month.
However, Costa argues that the issue is more complex and regulators might be working toward targeted changes. "First, regulators are escalating the financial stakes, shifting toward massive penalties like Anthropic's $1.5 billion and Meta's $1.4 billion settlements."
Additionally, a major challenge right now is actually enforceability — particularly as some companies have already been exploiting loopholes to avoid paying fines. Clearview AI, for example, managed to avoid paying $105 million in fines imposed by four different European regulatory authorities by arguing that it did not fall within European jurisdiction.
"Even if these early fines are manageable for tech giants, their real value lies in establishing the firm legal precedents that will govern how AI must operate in the future," Costa concludes.
Silvia Iacovcich is a tech journalist with over five years of experience in the field, including AI, cybersecurity, and fintech. She has written for various publications focusing on the evolving regulatory landscape of AI, digital behavior, web3, and blockchain, as well as social media privacy and security regulations.

articles.title: Beehiiv creators are buzzing about a new price increase
articles.text:
Beehiiv, a creator platform that has risen in popularity as an alternative to Substack, is increasing its prices — and many users aren’t happy. In a post explaining the increase, Beehiiv cofounder and CEO Tyler Denk says it will allow the company to “continue investing in our core platform experience.”
Beehiiv creators are buzzing about a new price increase
Creators may have escaped the Substack tax, but now they’re facing a price increase of at least $10 per month.
As part of the change, Beehiiv is changing the name of its midrange Scale plan to Lite, which has gone up by at least $10 per month depending on subscriber count. For someone with up to 10,000 subscribers, for example, Beehiiv will charge $139 / month instead of $109. Meanwhile, the Pro plan (formerly Max) will cost $239 / month for up to 10,000 subscribers, a jump from the previous $219 /month price. Creators with less than 2,500 subscribers can continue using Beehiiv for free.
The price hike has several creators on social media reconsidering their decision to use the platform, which many have joined to avoid the 10 percent cut Substack takes from total subscription revenue. In a post on Bluesky, freelance journalist Tim Stevens expresses frustration with the changes to Beehiiv that he’s seen after switching to the platform earlier this year. “Since then, the sponsor choices and ad rates have tanked.” Stevens writes. “Now, Beehiiv is hiking its fees 25%, making this an even less profitable endeavor.”
Matt Lombardo, who also recently moved his NFL news site Between the Hashmarks from Substack to Beehiiv, mentioned his issues with the change as well. “Beehiiv raising prices without yet offering video podcasts, a viable consistent growth engine on platform, or podcast ads is pretty frustrating to experience, as someone who enjoys the platform,” Lombardo writes on Threads.
In a post on Reddit, Extra Points creator Matt Brown notes that while he believes Beehiiv is a “steal” compared to Substack, he acknowledges that this “really isn’t true for many other publishers,” especially for those who don’t charge a subscription fee for their work:
As these prices increase, I think it’s becoming increasingly clear that if you have under 10K subscribers and rely on Beehiiv to do the majority of your rev-gen, and ESPECIALLY if you’re outside the United States, the answer is going to be No. It isn’t worth it. You’ll be able to get similar functionality at a lower startup cost, and can plug in affilate ads via other networks.
Beehiiv has differentiated itself from other platforms by offering a trove of built-in features, including an integrated ad network, website personalization options, and podcast creation tools. The company recently launched a new feature that allows creators to build a community into their website. “It’s only the second time we’ve ever updated our plans and pricing in beehiiv’s near five year history,” Denk writes. “Over the past several years, we have greatly expanded the capabilities of the platform.”

articles.title: Tesla sustains its EV sales momentum despite US troubles | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Tesla sold more than 480,000 EVs in the third quarter, as the company continues finding ways to move new cars despite its troubles in the U.S. market.
It was the second strong quarter in a row for Tesla after a somewhat rough start to the year. The sales figure easily beat out consensus estimates from Wall Street and topped even the most optimistic view for the company, which made its 10 millionth vehicle earlier this year.
The company said Friday morning that it built 464,391 vehicles in the quarter and delivered more than 486,532. That’s an increase of roughly 6,000 vehicle deliveries compared to the second quarter. But sales were still down from the same period last year, when Tesla delivered 497,000 vehicles. That quarter — Tesla’s best ever — was helped by a rush of U.S. buyers who were looking to take advantage of an expiring federal tax credit.
Before Friday’s numbers were released, Tesla’s sales were down nearly 20% year-over-year in the U.S. market, according to Cox Automotive.
That drop has been the result of a number of factors. Tesla has not released any new consumer models in years — with the exception of the Cybertruck, which has been a commercial flop. Potential buyers have also balked because of Elon Musk’s personal support of Donald Trump’s presidential campaign and his role overseeing the Department of Government Efficiency, which laid off thousands of workers and canceled international aid funding.
Tesla has looked to other markets to make up for lost U.S. sales. The company’s sales are on the rise again in Europe, where EVs are more widely adopted and supported by tighter emissions regulations. Tesla is reportedly expanding capacity at its factory in Germany to meet that demand. The company has also seen continued strong sales out of its factory in China despite competition in the region, with some of those sales driven by Tesla looking to newer markets like Japan, Australia, and Lithuania.
Despite the rebound in overall momentum, sales have become something of a taboo subject for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who is increasingly focused on the company’s other efforts. Perhaps the biggest example is the Cybercab, which Tesla started putting on the roads of Austin, Texas in recent weeks. The two-seater EV has been giving autonomous rides to passengers despite having no driver, steering wheel, or pedals.
Tesla also recently launched the production version of its electric big rig, nearly a decade after it was first introduced. The company aims to make roughly 50,000 Tesla Semi vehicles per year.
Other new efforts are in the works, but don’t have firm commercial timelines. The second-generation Roadster is set to be re-revealed on October 15 after years of delays, though it’s not clear when it will get built. Tesla is also developing the Optimus humanoid robot, but has repeatedly pushed back its timeline. Earlier this week, Tesla announced it had secured up to $30 billion in new lines of credit to support these projects.

articles.title: Medical records giant Epic pauses product development to fix security bugs that risk patients' data | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Epic, the software technology giant that makes the widely used MyChart software for accessing patients’ medical data, has paused most of its product development as the company works to protect its software and systems from cyberattacks.
Judy Faulkner, the founder and chief executive of Epic, told Modern Healthcare last month that the pause would likely last six weeks while work continues on “safeguarding” the company’s products, after a deployment of Anthropic’s frontier cybersecurity model Mythos unearthed security flaws that could allow access to patients’ data.
The company has not disclosed the nature of the bugs, but its chief security officer Stirling Martin told The New York Times that some customer configurations of MyChart could allow outsiders to access patient records without recording any intrusion in the software’s logs.
Martin, who did not return TechCrunch’s request for comment, told the Times that the AI model did not say if the bug could be exploited to alter patient records without detection, but argued it was enough of a risk to remediate the issues.
Epic’s widely used MyChart software is used to maintain over 320 million patient records across hospitals and doctor’s offices across the United States. Epic says it does not have access to customers’ medical data: that responsibility falls on healthcare providers like hospitals and doctor’s offices. But a bug unknown to Epic could allow hackers to compromise multiple MyChart affected systems located across the United States and raid the data stored within.
It’s rare for a company to pause development to fix security bugs, but the advent of AI tools capable of rapidly finding and exploiting security vulnerabilities has led to concerns that attackers could have an easier time at stealing data.
Healthcare breaches are increasingly common as hackers seek access to highly sensitive health and medical data, under the assumption that providers would pay to prevent hackers from publishing the information online. A 2024 ransomware attack on Change Healthcare, a health tech company owned by insurance giant UnitedHealth tasked with handling payments and billing for most Americans, allowed hackers to steal health data on more than 192 million people, the majority of people in the United States. The company paid the hackers twice not to publish the stolen data.
This year, a string of back-to-back data breaches at healthcare and tech companies have affected tens of millions of Americans. This includes medical records stolen during a breach at electronic health data storage giant CareCloud, millions of rows of patient data from pharmaceutical distributor McKesson, and an unspecified amount of stolen data from U.K.-based health tech company Craneware, whose software is used across North America.
The Department of Health and Human Services currently lists a breach at dental insurance company DentaQuest affecting 15 million people as the largest healthcare-related data breach of 2026 so far.

articles.title: Continuous Health Monitoring Drives Integrated Wearable System Design - EE Times
articles.text:
The smaller a wearable electronics gadget gets, the more it has to do. A device that once tracked steps and heart rate now has to continuously capture physiological signals while making room for more sensors, optics, processing, and power management. That is pushing wearable designers to treat the optical, mechanical, sensing, and power domains as a connected system, rather than designing each function separately.
“We are seeing a lot of integration happening in devices,” said Praveen Jose, senior technical leader, field applications, at Analog Devices India, during a press briefing organized by the company. “Your devices become smaller and smaller, but the quality of the devices or the quality of the performance is increasing.”
Jose said the challenge is how to accommodate more functions within a small device and make it a single-body solution.
Sensio, an Indian startup developing smart rings, smart bands, and patches, focuses on wellness and health and claims its wearables collect heart rate, respiratory rate, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, and activity data.
At the press briefing, Venkatesh Vadde, co-founder and CEO of Sensio, described how electrocardiogram (ECG) and photoplethysmography (PPG) can be used to estimate blood pressure continuously without a cuff, although he noted that the approach does not provide absolute blood pressure.
He said the startup works on embedding sensors in wearable devices, placing them at the right point, optimizing the signal, and using algorithms to interpret raw physiological signals.
That puts the optical path, sensor position, and physical construction of the wearable closer to the semiconductor design problem. Vadde said Sensio works with ADI sensors and other components and optimizes sensor placement, housing, and optics as part of the wearable design.
Identifying the problems
Jose said that optical sensing is challenging because the required physiological signal is embedded in noise. The sensing system needs to capture the required signal in the presence of noise before the data can be processed by algorithms or AI.
“In that particular scenario, you need to have a very good device which can actually sense the data in the presence of noise,” he said. “How accurately you can sense it is what will give you better data.”
For a wearable designer, that means the optical assembly, sensor position, and mechanical construction can affect the quality of the electrical signal coming from the sensor. Vadde highlighted how closely the mechanical and optical aspects of the wearable are linked to PPG performance. The placement of the optical assembly relative to the skin affects the signal.
“Even a fraction of a millimeter lift-off of the optical assembly from the skin impacts PPG,” Vadde said.
The enclosure, housing, skin contact, optical assembly, and sensor placement therefore all have a bearing on the signal ultimately processed by the device.
For a ring, this becomes particularly important because the device has to maintain consistent contact with the skin while remaining small enough to be worn continuously, including during sleep.
The same system-level problem appears when the wearer moves. Vadde said motion artefacts, power consumption, and signal quality are real design challenges in wearable devices. The optics, mechanics, and housing have to be considered together.
This brings an accelerometer or inertial measurement unit (IMU) into the physiological sensing chain. In a consumer wearable, an accelerometer can be used to determine activity or movement. In a health-monitoring wearable, motion information can also help identify periods when another physiological measurement may be affected by motion artefacts.
Vadde said an IMU can be used to screen motion artefacts so that the system accepts higher-quality physiological data.
Jose described motion and activity detection as one of the functions being integrated into wearable platforms. “When we have something that we want to monitor, what we want to have is the motion to be sensed,” he said.
The signal quality can also affect power consumption. Vadde pointed to automatic gain control (AGC) as an example. When optical coupling or motion affects the quality of the signal, the system can increase the gain to recover the required signal. Depending on the implementation, that can also affect power consumption.
This creates a chain of interdependent design decisions—optical and mechanical design affect signal quality; signal quality affects analog processing and gain; processing affects power consumption; and power consumption affects battery life.
The power architecture also has to account for sensing frequency, processing, connectivity, and periods when the device does not need to operate at full activity. “Sometimes what happens is, when a person is taking rest, and we know that during different conditions more power is needed by the product, we will go into sleep mode or deep sleep mode, and the effect is to retain the battery power,” Jose said.
Connectivity is another consideration. Jose described the requirement as low-power to medium-power connectivity for continuous monitoring applications.
The frequency at which measurements are taken also affects battery life. Vadde said the required frequency of vital-sign measurements depends on the patient and the context. Taking measurements less frequently can extend battery life, while storing and synchronizing data rather than continuously transmitting it can also affect power consumption.
Combining sensing and power functions
The system-level problem is also shaping the way ADI approaches wearable customers. Vivek Tyagi, managing director, sales and country leader, at Analog Devices India, said the company sees two distinct types of customers: those with the capability to integrate optical components and those that require an easier-to-integrate approach.
Tyagi said the company has developed two types of solutions: sensor-hub devices that are easier for customers to use, and standalone solutions that he said can provide higher accuracy but require customers to have greater precision in integrating the optics, LEDs, and other elements.
ADI is also working on integrating sensing, power management, charging, and battery management functions. The company is also working on low-power solutions for applications such as continuous glucose monitoring. With ADI’s work on energy harvesting, mechanical movement or a temperature gradient can be converted into a small amount of electrical power that can be used to charge the device and extend battery life.
Jose said ADI’s solutions cover PPG, temperature sensing, ECG, and accelerometers, alongside power and connectivity functions.
For ring applications, Jose referred to Analog Devices MAX86178, while Vikash Singh, product application staff engineer, Healthcare Marketing and Applications, at Analog Devices India, described the MAX86184 as a small-form-factor PPG analog front end (AFE) designed for ring applications, with support for up to 14 LEDs and four photodiodes and dual-channel capability.
The MAX86178 is a more broadly integrated vital-sign analog front end (AFE) that combines PPG, ECG, and BioZ functions; its PPG section supports up to six LEDs and four photodiode inputs.
ADI is trying to bring more of the functions required by the wearable into fewer devices, while leaving customers with different levels of integration depending on their optical and system-design capabilities.
Tyagi said ADI is engaging customers earlier in their product roadmaps to understand what they want to build two or three years ahead and then co-create solutions.
“Then engage with a strategic partnership early on in their design journey, so that we can co-create a solution,” he said.
The sensing chain becomes the design problem
The trend toward continuous health monitoring is changing what has to be considered when designing a wearable.
Temperature sensors have to fit within small form factors while maintaining accuracy. Optical sensors have to extract physiological signals from noisy environments. Mechanical construction and sensor placement affect optical coupling. Motion information can be used to identify artefacts. Analog processing can compensate for weak signals but may affect power consumption. Connectivity has to transmit or synchronize the resulting data without exhausting the battery.
Jose said the quality of the sensed data is central to continuous monitoring. “How accurately you can sense it is what will give you better data,” he said.
For wearable designers, the implication is that the sensing problem extends beyond an individual sensor. Optical and mechanical design, motion sensing, analog processing, algorithms, connectivity, and power all affect how a wearable collects and handles physiological data over time.
As wearables move from tracking activity toward continuous health monitoring, the engineering challenge is increasingly how these functions work together inside a device with very little room for error and physical space.

articles.title: Cómo usar tu móvil como una cámara profesional sin gastar más
articles.text:
Cómo usar tu móvil como una cámara profesional sin gastar más
Los teléfonos tienen más posibilidades fotográficas de las que probablemente utilizas. Con algunos ajustes y una buena composición puedes conseguir resultados mucho mejores
Hace tiempo que dejamos de necesitar una cámara específica para realizar buenas fotografías. De hecho, suelen ser pocos los que las llevan ya en sus viajes o eventos: el móvil se ha convertido en el dispositivo para todo que llevamos siempre encima y cuyos resultados fotográficos pueden llegar a ser muy profesionales. Pero para conseguirlos no basta con pulsar el botón de disparo; de hecho, la clave está en dejar de usar siempre la cámara en automático y aprovechar las opciones manuales que tienen ya todos los dispositivos. Estos son algunos de los ajustes y trucos que harán que consigas las mejores fotografías.
Lo primero: limpia la lente
Parece una tontería, pero es probablemente uno de los trucos más efectivos y una de las cosas que menos hacemos. Y es que el teléfono pasa buena parte del día en un bolsillo, un bolso o apoyado sobre diferentes superficies, así que la lente de la cámara acaba acumulando huellas y polvo que pueden provocar fotografías menos nítidas, reflejos o zonas con aspecto ligeramente borroso. Por eso, antes de hacer una foto importante debes limpiar las cámaras con un paño suave, preferiblemente de microfibra, sin aplicar ningún producto.
No utilices siempre el zoom digital
Cuando usas zoom pellizcando la pantalla no sabes qué cámara está utilizando realmente el teléfono. Hay que tener en cuenta que los móviles actuales suelen incorporar varias: principal, ultra gran angular, teleobjetivo… Cuando seleccionamos determinadas ampliaciones, el teléfono puede cambiar entre ellas, recurrir al recorte o al procesamiento digital sin que lo sepamos. Por eso, si quieres obtener la mejor calidad posible, es preferible utilizar los aumentos ópticos.
Y hay un truco muy sencillo que puedes hacer con cualquier móvil: antes de hacer la fotografía, prueba a moverte unos pasos hacia delante o hacia atrás. A veces el cambio de perspectiva mejora la imagen más que aumentar el zoom.
Controla la exposición
El móvil hace un trabajo extraordinario calculando automáticamente la exposición, pero hay situaciones en las que puede equivocarse con respecto a lo que queremos conseguir. Por ejemplo, si estamos fotografiando a una persona delante de una ventana, es posible que la cámara interprete que hay demasiada luz y oscurezca el rostro. También puede ocurrir lo contrario con una escena muy oscura. Esto se soluciona controlando la exposición: es preferible conservar detalle en una zona muy iluminada que acabar con un cielo completamente blanco o una ventana sin ningún detalle.
Si tu móvil tiene modo Pro, aprende a utilizar ISO y velocidad
Aquí es donde realmente podemos empezar a acercarnos a los controles de una cámara convencional. Los iPhone y algunos teléfonos Android incluyen un modo Pro o Manual con el que modificar parámetros como ISO, velocidad de obturación, enfoque y balance de blancos. También existen aplicaciones de cámara que ofrecen estos controles cuando el hardware del teléfono lo permite (Lightroom, por ejemplo). Pero, ¿para qué sirve cada uno?
El ISO determina la sensibilidad que aplicamos a la captura: subirlo puede resultar útil cuando hay poca luz, pero también introducir más ruido en la imagen. La velocidad de obturación, por otro lado, determina durante cuánto tiempo se captura la luz. Asimismo, una velocidad rápida ayuda a congelar el movimiento; una lenta permite captar más luz, aunque cualquier movimiento puede provocar una fotografía movida. De ahí que, para fotografiar a un niño corriendo, un animal o una persona en movimiento, interese utilizar una velocidad lo suficientemente rápida. Para una escena nocturna estática, en cambio, una velocidad más lenta ayuda a conseguir una imagen más luminosa. Prueba a jugar con estos ajustes y observa cómo cambia la imagen.
El enfoque también se puede controlar
Otra de las funciones que solemos dejar completamente en manos del teléfono es el enfoque. En una fotografía sencilla no hay ningún problema: apuntamos y el móvil encuentra automáticamente el sujeto. Pero si hay varios elementos a diferentes distancias, es probable que acabe enfocando algo distinto de lo que queríamos. Tocar sobre el sujeto permite indicar al teléfono dónde queremos enfocar.
Activa la cuadrícula
Su función no es hacer mejores fotografías automáticamente, sino ayudarte a componerlas. Las líneas permiten comprobar si el horizonte está recto y facilitan colocar los elementos importantes de la imagen. Y aquí entra en juego una regla clásica de composición: la regla de los tercios. Consiste en imaginar la imagen dividida en nueve partes mediante dos líneas horizontales y dos verticales y colocar los elementos importantes cerca de sus intersecciones.
No necesitas disparar siempre a máxima resolución
Otro error bastante habitual es pensar que cuantos más megapíxeles tenga una fotografía, mejor será. Los modos de máxima resolución pueden ser útiles cuando necesitamos conservar más detalle y queremos recortar posteriormente, pero también generan archivos de mayor tamaño. Para las fotografías del día a día no siempre tiene sentido utilizar la máxima resolución disponible. Reserva esa opción para situaciones en las que realmente puedas aprovecharla.
Si tienes RAW, úsalo… pero no para todo
Algo similar ocurre con el formato RAW; uno de los recursos más interesantes si después vas a editar tus fotografías. A diferencia de un JPEG o HEIF procesado, un archivo RAW conserva mucha más información de la captura y proporciona mayor margen para modificar posteriormente parámetros como exposición, color y balance de blancos. Pero hay una pega: los archivos son mucho más grandes. Por eso, no se recomienda utilizar RAW para todas las fotografías. Para una fotografía que quieres editar con cuidado, tiene mucho sentido.

articles.title: Decathlon casse le prix de ses vélos de route électriques haut de gamme Van Rysel E-EDR AF
articles.text:
Les vélos de route électriques occupent une place un peu à part dans l’univers du vélo à assistance électrique (VAE). Plus légers et plus discrets que les vélos électriques classiques, ils cherchent à conserver les sensations d’un vélo de route tout en ajoutant un petit coup de pouce dans les montées ou lorsque les jambes commencent à fatiguer. Ils permettent de profiter de l’assistance sans avoir l’impression de rouler sur un deux-roues de 25 kg.
Chez Decathlon, le Van Rysel SRAM Apex AXS 1x12v passe aujourd’hui à 1 599,99 € au lieu de 2 799,99 €, soit 1 200 € de réduction. Une seconde version, équipée d’une transmission Shimano 105 2x11S, profite également d’une remise et passe à 1 799,99 € au lieu de 2 449,99 €.
Decathlon écoule ici des fins de série. Ces prix s’appliquent depuis le 31 août 2026, jusqu’à épuisement des stocks.
C’est quoi, ce vélo électrique de route ?
L’E-EDR AF est un vélo de route à assistance électrique construit autour d’un cadre en aluminium (« AF » pour Aluminium Frame). Ce choix permet à Van Rysel de contenir le poids et le prix, avec un vélo annoncé à moins de 14 kg en taille M. Pour un vélo de route électrique, c’est plutôt léger, et cela se ressent surtout lorsqu’il faut le porter : monter quelques étages avec un VAE de 20 kg n’a pas exactement le même charme.
Le cadre adopte une géométrie typée endurance et s’accompagne d’une fourche entièrement en carbone. Les deux versions disposent également de pneus de 32 mm, de roues en aluminium compatibles tubeless et de freins à disque hydrauliques avec des disques de 160 mm à l’avant comme à l’arrière. L’assistance repose dans les deux cas sur le Mahle X35, installé dans le moyeu arrière, jusqu’à 40 Nm de couple. Trois niveaux d’assistance sont disponibles.
La version actuellement proposée à 1 599,99 € reçoit un SRAM Apex AXS électronique à 12 vitesses et mono-plateau. Le changement de vitesse est donc électronique et sans fil au niveau du dérailleur arrière. L’autre E-EDR AF, affiché à 1 799,99 €, utilise pour sa part un Shimano 105 mécanique à 11 vitesses et double plateau 50/34. Ce dernier, plus traditionnel, conviendra davantage aux cyclistes qui préfèrent retrouver les sensations et les habitudes d’une transmission de vélo de route classique.
À ce prix, les Van Rysel E-EDR AF sont-ils une bonne affaire ?
Les deux versions partagent le même moteur, la même batterie et le même cadre. Seule la transmission les distingue. Le SRAM Apex AXS coûte actuellement 200 € de moins et profite surtout d’une remise beaucoup plus importante : 1 200 € contre 650 € pour le Shimano 105. Le SRAM est ainsi particulièrement intéressant pour qui veut profiter de la promotion tout en passant à une transmission électronique à 12 vitesses. Le Shimano conserve, lui, l’intérêt d’une transmission mécanique à double plateau, plus familière pour les habitués du vélo de route.
Dans les deux cas, Decathlon vend un vélo de route électrique de moins de 14 kg, qu’on porte sans peine dans un escalier, pour moins de 1 600 € (ou moins de 1 800 € selon le modèle). À ce prix, c’est une très bonne affaire. Decathlon annonce jusqu’à 100 km d’autonomie dans les conditions les plus favorables pour les deux modèles.

articles.title: 700 kg d'appui et un look de Formule 1 : les secrets fous de l’aileron du futur Tesla Roadster
articles.text:
Le nouveau Tesla Roadster a encore une fois été retardé, avec une présentation maintenant reportée au 15 octobre. Le mauvais temps est visiblement en cause en empêchant une démonstration en plein air du véhicule… Car selon les dernières rumeurs, le Roadster pourra décoller grâce au pack SpaceX ajoutant un quatuor de propulseurs au dos de l’engin. De quoi faire perdre les pédales au premier farfelu qui en prendra le volant.
Ou pas, car la marque américaine semble avoir prévu le coup en intégrant une ribambelle de garde-fous. Électroniques, bien entendu, avec le traditionnel antipatinage, mais aussi aérodynamiques, par un aileron XXL qui empêchera au Roadster de quitter la terre ferme par inadvertance. Une nouvelle demande de brevet montre ainsi ce dernier élément segmenté en deux parties.
Un aileron high-tech digne d’une Formule 1
Contrairement à certains modèles jouant sur le spectaculaire, l’aileron du Roadster sera élégamment intégré à la carrosserie pour une meilleure fluidité des lignes lorsque le véhicule est à l’arrêt ou en usage normal. Cela ne l’empêchera pas d’être particulièrement efficace en situation de course car ce dernier pourra générer jusqu’à 700 kg d’appui aérodynamique. Suffisant pour garantir une belle stabilité en toutes circonstances.
La partie avant de l’aileron se caractérise par sa petite lamelle effleurant le couvercle du coffre. Celle-ci permet de masquer la jonction entre l’aileron et la carrosserie afin de préserver le style du véhicule. Le déploiement de l’ensemble est permis par quatre vérins fixés sur le coffre. Pilotés de manière indépendante, ces derniers peuvent complètement modifier le profil aérodynamique du Roadster en inclinant l’aileron.
Une aérodynamique active et ultra-réactive
La marque avance d’ailleurs une belle réactivité du système en pouvant passer de la position repliée à la position déployée en l’espace de 3 secondes. L’angle peut d’autre part être modifié en moins d’un quart de seconde. Un contrôleur gèrera automatiquement l’ensemble en fonction de la vitesse, de l’accélération, de l’angle du volant, du freinage, de la position GPS et des données de la conduite autonome.
L’élément est ainsi en position horizontale en ligne droite et se déploie en prenant de l’angle lors des freinages appuyés, ou en courbes rapides. Mieux, l’aileron peut lui-même passer en mode circuit si le GPS détecte une entrée sur piste. Cette pièce dépassant particulièrement à l’arrière du véhicule, deux systèmes de sécurité permettent de limiter la casse lors d’un usage sur route.
Lorsqu’un impact dépassant un certain seuil de force est détecté, l’aileron se replie rapidement afin de ne pas blesser un piéton ou un cycliste par exemple. Lorsqu’un risque de collision est détecté par les caméras du véhicule, le système se range également avant l’éventuel choc. Tous ces éléments apportent donc de beaux indices sur le nouveau Roadster, qui sera autant capable d’épater la galerie que de garder les pieds sur terre.

articles.title: Ya es oficial: estos son los nuevos auriculares Logitech que podrás reparar con recambios vendidos en España
articles.text:
Compro unos auriculares, los utilizo durante unos cuantos años y se agrietan las almohadillas, se rompe su diadema o la batería ya no aguanta lo que debería. En muchos casos esto supone que compremos unos nuevos o que sustituyamos una de sus piezas, generalmente a través de partes vendidas por otras marcas que no quedan igual o no funcionan de la misma forma.
Logitech quiere acabar con ello lanzando los Zone Vibe Pro, unos auriculares que, entre muchas otras cosas, cuenta con recambios que se podrán comprar a través de su tienda en el caso de que los necesitemos.
Logitech Zone Vibe Pro
Una forma de prolongar su vida útil
Los Logitech Zone Vibe Pro son unos auriculares supraaurales que tienen un diseño bastante minimalista y elegante. Vienen sin brazo de micrófono porque su objetivo es utilizarse tanto en el trabajo como en cualquier otro escenario. Vienen, además, con certificación para Microsoft Teams, Zoom y Google Meet.
A nivel interno incorporan altavoces de 40 mm y disponen de cancelación activa de ruido adaptable para un uso tanto en interiores como, sobre todo, en exteriores para así tener una mayor inmersión en todo momento. También cuentan con una diadema acolchada para poder utilizarlos durante varias horas.
En cuanto a la batería, ofrece hasta 30 horas de reproducción o 18 de conversación con la cancelación activa de ruido. Si la desactivamos, la autonomía alcanza las 66 horas. Además, con cinco minutos de carga da una autonomía de hasta una hora de conversación. Incluso todas las funciones se pueden utilizar mientras se recarga su batería a través del puerto USB-C.
Pero sin duda alguna, uno de los puntos más interesantes es el de la posibilidad de sustituir la diadema, las almohadillas y la batería en el futuro para prolongar la vida útil, un aspecto fundamental para aquellos momentos en los que no podamos tramitar la garantía porque esta ha finalizado.
Los auriculares de Logitech ya están a la venta en varios modelos:
- Logitech Zone Vibe Pro por un precio de 259,99 euros.
- Logitech Zone Vibe Pro for Business (incluye un receptor Zone USB-C) por un precio de 279,99 euros.

articles.title: GTA VI sur un écran OLED : 4 TV et moniteurs en promotion chez PcComponentes — Frandroid
articles.text:
Quand on parle d’un bon setup de jeu, on pense d’abord à la machine : console ou PC, puissance, carte graphique, processeur… C’est logique. Mais une configuration musclée ne suffit pas si l’affichage n’est pas à la hauteur. Un bon setup passe aussi par un écran capable de rendre justice au travail des développeurs, avec une image propre, réactive et fluide.
Sur ce terrain, l’OLED a de sérieux arguments. Noirs profonds, contraste élevé, couleurs justes, réactivité : il coche beaucoup de cases pour profiter des jeux récents dans les meilleures conditions possibles. C’est justement là qu’interviennent PcComponentes et ses Jours orangés. Jusqu’au 11 octobre, l’enseigne propose plusieurs TV et moniteurs OLED à prix réduit. De quoi préparer l’arrivée de GTA VI tout en profitant dès maintenant des gros jeux du moment.
Les meilleures offres OLED des Jours orangés :
- le TV Samsung OLED TQ55S90HAEXXC à 999 € au lieu de 1 079 € ;
- le TV LG OLED evo OLED55G64LW à 1 536 € au lieu de 1 823 € ;
- le moniteur AOC AGON AG27QZD2 à 427 € ;
- le moniteur MSI MPG 321URXW à 742 € au lieu de 849 €.
Samsung OLED TQ55S90HAEXXC : le TV gaming polyvalent
Avec le TQ55S90HAEXXC, Samsung propose une télé OLED qui mise sur la polyvalence, capable de répondre aussi bien aux usages classiques d’un téléviseur de salon qu’à ceux d’un gamer exigeant. Le téléviseur embarque une dalle OLED 4K de 55 pouces (parfaite pour les pièces avec environ 2 mètres de recul), épaulée par le processeur NQ4 AI Gen3, qui se charge notamment de l’upscaling 4K et des différents traitements d’image. Le HDR10+ Gaming, le Dolby Atmos, Q-Symphony ou encore OTS Lite sont aussi de la partie pour soigner l’expérience audiovisuelle, quel que soit le contenu visionné.
Samsung n’a pas non plus oublié les joueurs. La présence de quatre ports HDMI 2.1 permet de profiter des principales technologies d’affichage du moment, comme le VRR (pour réduire le tearing), l’ALLM (pour réduire la latence), ainsi que G-Sync et FreeSync Premium Pro pour la synchronisation adaptative. La fluidité est également au rendez-vous avec un taux de rafraîchissement natif de 100 Hz, qui peut grimper jusqu’à 165 Hz en VRR grâce au Motion Xcelerator 165 Hz. De quoi largement répondre aux besoins des consoles actuelles, mais aussi rendre ce téléviseur intéressant si l’on souhaite directement y brancher un PC gaming.
La présence du traitement Glare Free, qui vise à réduire les reflets, est également appréciable si l’on souhaite installer le TQ55S90HAEXXC dans une pièce lumineuse. Pendant les Jours orangés, PcComponentes propose ce téléviseur à 999 € au lieu de 1 079 €, un tarif intéressant pour découvrir les avantages de l’OLED sur un grand écran.
TV LG OLED evo OLED55G64LW : l’OLED qui mise sur la luminosité
S’ils partagent la même diagonale, le TV OLED evo OLED55G64LW se démarque du modèle proposé par Samsung par un positionnement plus premium, qui mise avant tout sur la qualité d’image et le confort. Son point fort ? Le Brightness Booster Ultra, une fonctionnalité qui permet, selon le constructeur, d’obtenir un pic lumineux jusqu’à 3,9 fois supérieur à celui d’un téléviseur OLED de référence. L’ajout du traitement Reflection Free Premium, qui cherche à réduire les reflets tout en préservant la profondeur des noirs et l’intensité des couleurs, permet aussi à ce téléviseur de mieux s’adapter aux pièces lumineuses.
Côté image, LG a misé sur le processeur Alpha 11 AI 4K Gen3 et ses différents traitements, comme l’upscaling ou le Dynamic Tone Mapping Ultra, ainsi que sur les technologies HDR habituelles, avec le HDR10 et le HLG, auxquelles vient s’ajouter le Dolby Vision. Sur le plan audio, le Dolby Atmos et le système 4.2 canaux de 60 watts offrent également de belles prestations. Pour le jeu, LG annonce un taux de rafraîchissement natif de 120 Hz qui grimpe jusqu’à 165 Hz en VRR, un temps de réponse annoncé de 0,1 ms et la présence du Dolby Vision Gaming en 4K 120 Hz. S’y ajoutent les traditionnels VRR, ALLM, G-Sync et FreeSync Premium.
Côté prix, PcComponentes annonce une ristourne de 287 €, qui fait passer ce téléviseur OLED evo OLED55G64LW à 1 536 € au lieu de 1 823 €.
AOC AGON AG27QZD2 : le bon écran pour découvrir le QD-OLED
Si changer de téléviseur est hors budget, ou si vous souhaitez un écran QD-OLED utilisable aussi bien avec une console qu’avec un PC, l’AGON AG27QZD2 proposé par AOC possède de solides arguments. Côté affichage, sa dalle de 26,5 pouces en QHD et la certification DisplayHDR True Black 400 font leur part du travail : l’image est bien définie, avec des noirs profonds, un contraste élevé et une couverture colorimétrique étendue (99,1 % du gamut DCI-P3). La réactivité est également au rendez-vous, avec un taux de rafraîchissement qui grimpe jusqu’à 240 Hz via le DisplayPort, contre 144 Hz maximum en HDMI 2.0, et un temps de réponse annoncé de 0,03 ms gris à gris.
De manière assez classique pour un moniteur dédié au jeu, G-Sync Compatible et Adaptive-Sync sont présents pour limiter le tearing et les saccades. Selon AOC, le moniteur est également compatible avec les consoles en QHD jusqu’à 120 Hz. Le constructeur propose aussi une garantie de trois ans qui couvre le burn-in, à condition de respecter les conditions d’entretien prévues. Vous pouvez ainsi jouer l’esprit tranquille, même sur des jeux qui affichent longtemps des éléments fixes à l’écran, comme une minicarte ou une barre de vie.
Dernier atout dans l’escarcelle de l’AGON AG27QZD2 : son prix. Avec un tarif fixé à 427 €, ce moniteur affiche un rapport performances-prix intéressant pour découvrir les qualités du QD-OLED.
MSI MPG 321URXW : une dalle taillée pour les setups exigeants
Pour les joueurs disposant d’un budget confortable et souhaitant investir dans un bon moniteur QD-OLED, le MPG 321URXW constitue un choix cohérent. Sa dalle de 31,5 pouces en 4K UHD (3 840 × 2 160 pixels), son taux de rafraîchissement de 240 Hz, son temps de réponse gris à gris annoncé de 0,03 ms ou encore sa certification DisplayHDR True Black 400 sont autant d’arguments en sa faveur. L’image est fluide, contrastée et riche, y compris lorsque le contenu HDR se montre exigeant : MSI annonce un pic lumineux pouvant atteindre 1 000 nits sur une fenêtre de 3 %.
Le constructeur a également soigné la connectique de son écran afin de répondre à différents usages. L’USB-C avec DisplayPort Alt Mode et Power Delivery jusqu’à 90 watts est un vrai plus pour les utilisateurs de PC portable, tandis que les ports HDMI 2.1 permettent aux possesseurs de consoles de profiter pleinement des capacités de leur machine, notamment avec le VRR et l’ALLM.
Comme AOC, MSI accompagne son moniteur d’une garantie de trois ans qui couvre aussi le marquage de la dalle (burn-in). Vous pouvez donc profiter de ses 240 Hz sans arrière-pensée, même lors de longues sessions de jeu.
Pendant les Jours orangés, PcComponentes propose ce moniteur à 742 € au lieu de 849 €, soit une réduction de 107 €.

articles.title: Heiße Spur auf dem Mars: Dieses Mineral könnte von uraltem Leben erzählen
articles.text:
Nasa-Rover Perseverance analysiert 180 Ziele – und stößt auf einen Hinweis auf mikrobielles Leben
„Wenn es eine Sache gibt, die ich nach zehn Jahren Arbeit mit Mars-Rovern gelernt habe, dann ist es, dass der Mars einen ständig mit Überraschungen bombardiert“, sagte Candice Bedford in einer Pressemitteilung der Nasa.
Die Wissenschaftlerin der Purdue University in West Lafayette im US-Bundesstaat Indiana ist die Hauptautorin einer Studie, die gerade in der Zeitschrift Communications Earth & Environment erschienen ist.
Magmatisches Gestein anstatt Sedimente
Das Forschungsteam um Candice Bedford untersuchte Daten, die der Nasa-Rover Perseverance in der sogenannten Margin-Unit des Marskraters Jezero gesammelt hatte.
Beobachtungen aus dem Weltraum heraus hatten suggeriert, dass das Gestein der Margin-Unit aus Karbonat besteht, das sich durch die Wechselwirkung mit dem See gebildet hat, der früher in dem Krater lag. Doch statt Sedimentgestein entdeckten die Forscher:innen magmatisches Gestein.
Eine positive Überraschung, denn magmatisches Gestein gilt als optimale Zeitkapsel. Die darin enthaltenen Mineralkristalle lassen sich gut auf den Zeitpunkt ihrer Entstehung abklopfen.
Drei unterschiedliche Kontakte mit Wasser
Perseverance richtete seine sogenannte SuperCam auf das Gestein. Dieses Instrument kann anhand des Lichts, das von den Steinen reflektiert, dessen chemische Zusammensetzung erkennen. Auf diese Weise analysierte der Rover über 180 Ziele in dem Krater.
Das Resultat war überraschend: Das Gestein musste über gigantische Zeiträume drei Mal mit Wasser interagiert haben. Die Begegnungen veränderten seine chemische Beschaffenheit jedes Mal anders.
Das Wissenschaftsteam konnte die Abfolge der Kontakte mit Wasser bestimmen, die genauen Zeitpunkte aber nicht. Dazu müsste das Gestein auf der Erde analysiert werden.
Karbonatgrate und Siliziumdioxid
Beim ersten Aufeinandertreffen reagierte kohlendioxidreiches Grundwasser mit dem Mineral Olivin, das beim Abkühlen von Magma entstanden ist. Aus dem Kontakt entstanden Karbonatgrate.
Bei der zweiten Konfrontation war laut der Studie wohl der Kratersee involviert. Die Forschenden fanden Siliziumdioxid, das bei der Umwandlung von Olivin in Karbonat entsteht.
Fluorit deutet auf heißes Wasser hin
Die interessanteste Einsicht lieferte aber der dritte und historisch jüngste Kontakt von Gestein und Wasser. Dabei entstand nämlich Fluorit. Dieses Mineral bildet sich, wenn heißes Wasser mit vulkanischem Gestein reagiert. Dies deutet darauf hin, dass in dem Krater einmal eine Art Thermalquelle gelegen haben muss.
Hier wird es besonders spannend. Denn hydrothermale Systeme gelten als buchstäblich heiße Kandidaten als Brutstätte von Leben, wenn auch nur auf der Ebene von Mikroben. Dies macht die Margin-Unit zu einem Ort von astrobiologischem Interesse, wie es in der Studie heißt.

articles.title: Nacon’s new PS5 controller can mix audio from your phone and console
articles.text:
Nacon announced what the company is claiming is the world’s first officially licensed PlayStation 5 controller with a built-in screen for adjusting settings like joystick sensitivity or remapping buttons right on the gamepad. The Revolution 5 Unlimited’s screen can also be used to mix audio from multiple sources so while using a pair of headphones connected to the gamepad with a cable you can listen to music from your phone and sounds from the game you’re playing at the same time.
Nacon’s new PS5 controller can mix audio from your phone and console
The customizable Revolution 5 Unlimited gamepad features asymmetrical TMR thumbsticks and a built-in settings screen.
The Revolution 5 Unlimited is available for preorder starting today for $229.99 through Nacon’s online store and is expected to ship sometime later this year. While it’s primarily designed for use with the PS5, the R5U features an asymmetrical stick layout similar to Xbox and Switch gamepads with a pair of drift-resistant tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) thumbsticks. Both sticks can be customized by attaching alternate heads featuring different designs and the controller’s D-pad is swappable. You can use a classic four-way design or switch to an eight-way option that makes it easier to perform combo moves in fighting games.
Nacon even lets you adjust how balanced the controller feels with 10, 14, and 16 gram weights that can be inserted into the R5U’s non-slip grips.
On the top of the controller you’ll find a pair of shoulder buttons, a pair of customizable shortcut buttons, and a pair of triggers with adjustable travel that can be shortened to reduce reaction times in FPS games. There’s four additional customizable shortcut buttons on the back of the controller as well as a button used for quickly switching between multiple saved profiles.
The R5U is also compatible with PCs and Android devices and customizing its performance and functionality isn’t limited to its built-in screen. Nacon also offers a mobile app for iOS and Android that expands the customization options to include adjusting the thumbsticks’ response curves, tweaking EQ profiles for the audio sources, and modifying the color of the RGB lighting surrounding the right stick.

articles.title: Unidentified Flock Cameras in Florida - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Unidentified Flock Cameras in Florida
St. Lucie County in Florida discovered (alt link) a dozen Flock cameras whose ownership it can’t identify, and that the county government had not permitted.
I am reminded of the decade-old story of StingRay cell phone surveillance devices in Washington, DC, whose operators were also unknown.
My guess is that in the StingRay case, the devices were operated by foreign actors. This Flock case is more likely some local government entity that didn’t bother getting approval. Were I a foreign actor, I would rather hack the existing Flock network—like Israel did with Tehran’s surveillance cameras—than risk installing my own.
Regardless, once we normalize a surveillance infrastructure, both friends and foes will take advantage of it.
